speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON ASSISTANCE TO WESTERN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house I should like to make a statement regarding the western farm situation, which I undertook to do some two weeks ago and have since been awaiting the opportunity to place before the house the views of the government with regard to this matter.
Might I add that, as has been stated, following my statement, certain supplementary estimates will require to be brought to the attention of the house.
On August 30, 1958 I outlined the government's views concerning the development of a national agricultural policy, and pointed out that our concept of such a policy was based on the belief that the national welfare required positive action to meet the basic causes of maladjustment in particular industries and regions. Thus while the agricultural program was designed to be national in scope, it was necessary at all times to be concerned as well with specific regional problems. These regional policies in turn are required to form an integral part of and harmonize with the ends of national policy.
I do not intend to review the policy which I outlined on that occasion nor the achievements that have since been brought about under that policy. I referred to them in general on March 4, 1960. I would simply say that in connection with the broad national aspects of our planned agricultural policy,
the government's intention is to present to parliament further instalments at a subsequent session designed to round out the program which was announced in August, 1958.
On this occasion I wish to deal with one of the regional problems in agriculture which is a matter of particular national concern. I refer to the prairie farm income problem which has arisen from revolutionary changes in technology, world wheat demand conditions and rising costs of production. Partly because of dramatic technological development, more particularly because of the tremendous stimulus given to wheat production by virtually every importing and almost every exporting country, world surpluses have been built up to colossal proportions and the consequence has been a depressing effect on world prices for wheat.
The government has searched diligently for a solution to the question of farm prices which would avoid the evils built into the programs of other countries in recent years. Our determination has been to avoid a cure which would be worse than the disease itself. We have had the benefit of the opinion, in so far as the western grain problem is concerned, of the western members supporting the government, who have continued to place before us their views and have pressed for action in accordance with the situation.
The chief proposal which western farm organizations have advanced for dealing with this problem has been the so-called deficiency payment scheme on western grains. On previous occasions I have endeavoured to show how impossible this proposal would be in relation to a sound agricultural policy, realizing at the same time the necessity of agriculture being prosperous, without which the demands of agriculture or industrial production in other parts of Canada would be greatly reduced, with consequent loss of employment in other parts of Canada.
The summary of the views in this regard is this, as I stated in March, 1960. The government has come to the conclusion that deficiency payments, however attractive at first glance, would not provide a solution to the problems facing prairie agriculture but would indeed create new problems. Deficiency payments applied to deliveries of grain would fail to help those producers most in need and if adopted would require very large subsidies from the treasury, which would

Assistance to Western Farmers inevitably lead to increased surpluses and would add further to the burden of financing the disposal of those surpluses. Such payments would tend to impede essential adjustments to changing conditions of technology and demand which are essential both to the welfare of the producers and to the health of the Canadian economy as a whole.
In other words, the proposal of a fixed support type of deficiency payment would not solve the two main problems of western agriculture, that of income variability and the problem of the small farm. Indeed, it is the considered opinion of those with whom the government has consulted that in the long run the adoption of deficiency payments would have worsened those problems. Our national policy and indeed our regional policies are based on the fundamental principle of aiding rather than impeding essential adjustments to changing conditions of technology and demand.
A measure of assistance roughly analogous to unemployment insurance in industry is economically consistent with our basic policy of ensuring sound adjustments to changing conditions.
There is no way whereby, regardless of efficiency, a guaranteed annual income can be assured. As a result, our policy has consistently emphasized measures to attack the basic problems of agriculture; measures such as export assistance, crop insurance, a vastly improved and comprehensive agricultural credit policy, rural development, conservation and the like. We believe that the basic problems of Canadian agriculture will yield only to long range solutions. Since our national agricultural policy is designed to attack the basic problems of agriculture, I have always made it clear that some time must inevitably elapse before these long range solutions can be fully implemented and before their benefits will begin to raise the standard of farm living. I indicated in August, 1958 that some measure of special assistance to western farmers was justifiable and, as the house will recall, a measure of assistance was provided at that time.
I then discussed one form of special assistance which has always appealed to the members of the Conservative party. I refer to the two-price system. The proposal has seemed to me through the years to have a strong moral justification, while avoiding the dangers of other suggested remedies which, as I said a moment ago, might be a stimulus if not an invitation to increase and further surplus production. Indeed, such remedies among others have been proven to be the chief causes of the decline in world
[Mr. Diefenbaker.f
prices from which western farmers have suffered, as have farmers in other parts of the world.
Under the two-price system for wheat, the domestic price would be above the selling price for wheat on world markets as long as world markets remained substantially depressed. This proposal has quite properly been limited to wheat used for domestic human consumption, since any attempt to impose a domestic price on wheat for feed purposes would simply destroy the market and cause feeders to use other grains or feed products as a substitute. It could not, of course, apply to wheat produced for export. That would be financially impossible.
But attractive as the two-price system is, there have always been dangers and obstacles in the way of its implementation. Those who are primarily concerned with the maintenance and expansion of Canadian markets have pointed out that the establishment of a high domestic price would leave Canada in a vulnerable position when this country requests restraint on the part of other countries which subsidize wheat production and wheat exports. It has also been argued that as long as Canada is selling wheat to domestic consumers at the same price as it is willing to sell wheat abroad, no one can criticize the basis of our participation in export markets.
In opposition to this view, some farm organizations have over the years contended that the Canadian consumer has been getting wheat too cheaply. They argue that while the Canadian wheat producer must export his wheat at world prices, even if those prices are depressed, he should at least receive a fair price for that portion of his wheat sold in the domestic market for human consumption. They point historically, and with justification, to the unique burden imposed by government policy on wheat growers during the war and post-war years, resulting in domestic and export prices far below prevailing world levels.
This government, to fulfil its national and regional responsibilities, must take all points of view into account. On the one hand it must avoid doing anything that would impair the access of Canadian wheat to world markets, for if the world markets were lost nothing, and certainly not the Canadian government, could save the western wheat economy. On the other hand, the western farmers have a case against the continuation of a system in which the price of wheat sold for domestic consumption is set by depressed world prices.
This is a dilemma which this government has searched long and diligently to resolve. At times we have felt that in this search we

have received less constructive help from some western farm spokesmen than we might have expected. But be that as it may, we have been determined all along to resolve this dilemma and to extend a justifiable measure of assistance in a form which would not cause greater difficulties than those it was intended to resolve.
We have reached the conclusion that to attain the ends sought by the two-price system, while avoiding its inherent difficulties, the best way would be to bring about this year an acreage payment similar to that instituted in 1958. The government proposes, subject to the approval of parliament, to make an acreage payment of $1 per cultivated acre, up to a maximum of 200 acres, as shown in the western farmers' wheat board permit books. On the basis of the similar payment made in 1958, this will amount to between $41 and $42 million. This is an amount roughly equal to the average of what the western farmer would get if a two-price system for wheat were put into effect.
I wish now to say a word with regard to the liaison on committee. Since the government's rejection of deficiency payments in March the liaison committee of the western farm organizations has requested' a further meeting with the government to discuss alternatives to the form of assistance they had originally requested. Immediately after they made their first request in this regard they were communicated with and asked that they put in a specific alternative in writing so that it might be studied prior to the meeting. In doing this there was in no way an abdication on the part of the government of its responsibility. It was simply giving to them an opportunity to make their representation if they had such an alternative.
The reply we received was in the form of a brief dated May 10, which went into particulars on three proposals or arguments. The brief ended with a statement that the group were prepared to discuss acreage payments. The government will continue to give consideration to action which may be taken to meet the welfare not only of the western wheat farmer but farmers elsewhere in Canada. In so far as the former are concerned, we will meet with the liaison committee. I think it will be desirable that the three ministers from the western provinces meet with them. If desired I will join them to meet this committee so that its views may be secured in addition to any that were expressed in the brief to which I have made reference.
In concluding, I simply want to say that this proposal I have just presented will, I believe,
Assistance to Western Farmers bring about a measure of justifiable assistance this year to western growers. At the same time it will avoid doing anything that would impair the access of Canadian wheat to world markets or impede the necessary adjustments in the wheat economy resulting from the causes mentioned earlier. This is not a hand-out in any sense of the word. We hope this measure will not only provide some assistance in meeting a difficult regional problem but also, within the context of our national policy, a basis for a stronger economy in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it has not been easy to follow the words of the Prime Minister. Obviously he was embarrassed by the delay attending the announcement which he has made today. He sought to defend himself by a series of words which cannot be described other than to say they were understandably tortuous.
The Prime Minister is dealing with a matter today which will be discussed, of course, in considerable detail when the item on which it is based is presented to the house, but in view of the character of the announcement and its belated nature the Prime Minister, I know, will be among the first to expect me to say a word or two.

The Prime Minister says this is the first opportunity he has had to make this announcement. Of course the Prime Minister forgets easily-I know he does not forget intentionally-but a whole series of questions were addressed to him and to the Minister of Agriculture during the course of this session, all with the intention of trying to elicit from the government some reaction to the representations which were made by 1,000 western farmers over a year and a half ago. The announcement of today had its genesis in that mass movement of western farmers, who were met with a refusal by the government to accept their proposal for deficiency payments. The Prime Minister must be aware that in the brief presented at that time there were three other proposals of an alternative kind about which the government has made no comment whatsoever.
Since that time the Minister of Agriculture has stated on several occasions that the government's action was predicated on the submission by the western liaison committee of proposals which the government would consider; and having considered them, then an announcement would be made by the government, but not until the farmers of western

Assistance to Western Farmers Canada themselves had formulated a policy would this government itself decide on which policy it should embark.
This announced program of acreage assistance of $1 an acre up to a maximum of 200 acres, bringing the total cost to the federal treasury somewhere between $40 million and $41 million, as the Prime Minister noted, is precisely the same as the plan announced in 1958, but not pursued in 1959 by the government. The Prime Minister referred to the submissions made by the western liaison committee on May 10, and he said that in those submissions they had proposed acreage payments. It is significant that in the same submissions not only did they put forward that as an alternative plan, but they also requested an opportunity to meet with the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues to discuss the question at the Prime Minister's early convenience.
That was on May 10, and on August 8, 1960, the western liaison committee has not yet been given an opportunity to meet the government to present the requests made on May 10. It is no wonder that farm leaders all over western Canada, as we now know from the records of this house, have expressed their dissatisfaction with the government for refusing to meet with them to discuss alternative proposals. What we have today is not what the people of Canada were led to believe in 1957 the farmers would receive. This is not in line with the Prime Minister's declaration "Parity, not charity"; this is a policy of stand-off and hand-out, and there can be no denial of that fact.
I am sure the hon. member for Rosthern, who so courageously spoke up against the refusal of the government to live up to its election promises, will join with the many thousands of farmers in western Canada in protesting at the meagreness and insufficiency of this particular program. These farmers will remember the words of the Prime Minister when he said, "We will assure the farmer of his fair share of the national income by maintaining a flexible"-I underline the word "flexible"-"price support program to ensure parity for agricultural products based on a price-cost relationship". This program does not deal with the elimination of the cost squeeze. The Prime Minister today acknowledged the rise in the farmers' production costs.
This statement is made in the face of the fact that net farm income for 1959 is below that of 1958. This statement is made in the face of the fact that western farmers, as indeed all farmers in Canada, do not recognize in government policy, in government delays, in government procrastination, the realization of the assurances they were given.


The Prime Minister seeks to clothe this regrettable state of affairs with a so-called over-all policy. He says that further aspects of this policy will be discussed at the next session of parliament. He interlarded what he had to say by mentioning the fact that the government brought in crop insurance, forgetting of course that only one section of one province in Canada has thus far taken advantage of the federal plan.

I have always maintained that although one is elected by a constituency, he is responsible for having a knowledge and understanding of his province and his country, so I hope that what I have to say will be accepted as the view of this group on the important announcement that has just been made by the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister in opening his remarks told us that on August 28, 1958 the government's views on agricultural policy were made known. They were made known, sir, yes; but it was our understanding and, I think, the farmers' understanding that the government policy was one of parity, and so far we have not parity in agriculture. It is not until August 8 of this year that we have a further announcement by the Prime Minister on aid to agriculture, particularly regarding those whom we might classify as the western farmers.

Assistance to Western Farmers
I want to make clear right at the outset, sir, that any new policy or additional policy that is going to be of assistance to the farmers has the wholehearted support of this group. But it does not go far enough. That is an old term, but it has to be repeated time after time.
The Prime Minister spent a considerable amount of time, and perhaps understandably so, explaining to the house this afternoon why his government has put aside the idea of deficiency payments in favour of the proposal which is now before us, of $1 an acre payment with a maximum of $200. In view of the fact that the Prime Minister spent some time on that, we in this group would like to make our position known in commenting on the statement of the Prime Minister.
The farmers' case, Mr. Speaker, for deficiency payments is based on the fact that not only has the price of grain not increased, but in fact it has decreased since the end of the last world war. But in the meantime, sir, the cost of production has gone up, I understand by approximately 51 per cent. So to use -and I have no hesitation in using it-the phrase of the hon. member for Assiniboia, the farmer is caught in a price-cost squeeze.
As outlined by the Prime Minister, there are two ways of handling this, either to reduce the cost of production or to increase the price of the farmers' products. The Prime Minister has made it clear that there is no method which they have yet devised-and I rather think he stressed this-of being able to hold down the ever-increasing cost of agricultural production. It is because of this that the farmers have decided that a constructive alternative is to ask for an increase in prices through the medium of deficiency payments.
The Prime Minister has made it clear this afternoon that he has not only decided, but he is defending his government's policy of a $1 an acre payment, with a $200 maximum. He feels that is a better policy than deficiency payments. But, sir, a $1 an acre payment as suggested by the Prime Minister does very little to overcome the price-cost squeeze. Although he denied it-and I noticed that he denied it very emphatically-it still amounts to nothing more or less than a hand out or a relief measure.

I noticed that the Prime Minister emphasized aid to small farmers. He not only said it once; I think he said it three times. Two hundred dollars, in relation to a farmer's total expense and cost of living is, of course, most welcome; nevertheless it is a trivial sum, because a small farmer with less than 200 acres receives less than $200.
We say, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister and his government, by failing, as they have thus far, to control the farmers' cost of production are partially responsible for the present difficulties of the farmers. We say that by making deficiency payments, by establishing that policy, the government would be discharging its responsibility to the farmer to a greater measure than by the policy now outlined, because deficiency payments mean in effect an increase in the prices of wheat, oats and barley. They mean an increase to at least provide partial compensation for the increase in the cost of production. We say it is the major policy necessary to ensure the survival of the wheat industry, which is so important to the economy of our nation, and in particular to the economy of three of our western provinces.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he can make any report to the house on the situation in the Congo, or on that at the United Nations concerning the Congo?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONGO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed that the secretary general has reported to the security council on the implementation of the council's resolutions of July 14 and July 22, with particular reference to their application in the province of Katanga. Last week Dr. Bunche, with appropriate United Nations staff, travelled to that province to make arrangements for the peaceful entry of United Nations troops, planned for August 6. After consulting with the appropriate authorities in the province, Dr. Bunche returned to Leopoldville on August 6 to report to the secretary general.
Dr. Bunche recommended a halt in the Katanga operations of the United Nations because of the unyielding opposition of Premier Tshombe to the coming of United Nations troops and because of repeated warnings that they would be opposed by force. There was evidence that there would be opposition to the United Nations entry, which all along had been assumed to be a peaceful operation, consistent with the governing principles of the force which the secretary general had clearly stated.
Mr. Hammarskjold has now restated the United Nations position as follows. The force is not entitled to take such military initiative and action as, in view of what has now been made clear, would be necessary for an implementation of the security council decisions. The secretary general has now asked for instructions from the security council and for such decisions as the council may find appropriate in order to achieve its aims.
In this report he has stated that the aims of the resolutions cannot be achieved by the use of the United Nations force, as its mandate has been defined; that if the council wishes to maintain its objectives it must either change the character of the force, which to the secretary general appears impossible both for constitutional reasons and in view of the commitment to the contributing governments, or resort to other methods which would enable the secretary general to carry through the implementation without going beyond his instructions as regards the force.
The secretary general has made clear that the difficulty which the council faces in 79951-0-489
Inquiries of the Ministry Katanga does not have its root in the attitude of the Belgian government, which acquiesced in the security council decisions. Nor, it seems, is the problem one of a wish of the authorities of the province of Katanga too secede from the republic of Congo.
The secretary general states that the problem for those resisting the United Nations force in Katanga is that they consider United Nations participation in the control of security in the province would seriously jeopardize their possibility of working for other constitutional solutions than a strictly Unitarian one, that is, some kind of federal structure providing for a higher degree of provincial self government. The secretary general clearly regards this as an internal political problem to which the United Nations as an organization obviously cannot be a party. He asserts that the entry of the force into Katanga would not mean any taking of sides in the conflict, nor any shifting of political weights. He believes that all this can be avoided if the United Nations firmly maintains its aim and acts with clarity and tact. He has suggested that the security council may wish to clarify its views on the matter and to lay down such rules for the United Nations operation as would serve to separate effectively questions of a peaceful and democratic development in the constitutional field from any questions relating to the presence of the United Nations force.
This is the problem which the secretary general has laid before the security council and which it is considering at the present moment. The situation remains extremely delicate, and is rendered more complicated by demands for direct action by those whose interest in the Congo may not coincide with the aims of the United Nations.

speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Are reports accurate that the Soviet representative to the United Nations has questioned the propriety of Canada sending a contingent to this force?

Yes, Mr. Speaker; there has been some meddling in this regard. I am informed that on August 6 the Soviet representative in New York left a memorandum with the United Nations secretary general which argued that because Canada is a member of the NATO alliance, the despatch of Canadian troops to the Congo would be nothing else than assistance to an aggressor on the part of its military allies. This was described as a gross contradiction of the security council resolutions and, therefore, the Soviet union objected to the dispatch of Canadian troops.

Of course this Soviet charge is completely groundless. The government's decision to provide a Canadian contingent for the United Nations force was in direct response to a request for assistance by the secretary general, who has the responsibility for implementing the security council resolutions. Similar requests have been addressed to many other members of the United Nations, including other members of NATO.
Canada's firm support for the United Nations efforts to maintain peace is in no way inconsistent with our membership in NATO. If other members of the United Nations have differing views in this regard, it is their business to make them known to the secretary general. speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minisier of Trade and Commerce) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the report of the special committee appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the procedure in this house, presented Monday, July 25, 1960, be concurred in.
He said: I do not propose to speak at any great length with regard to this motion. Nevertheless, hon. members may wish to give attention to it because of the importance of the rules and procedure of the House of Commons.
I would point out at the outset that the proposals put forward are on a trial basis, suggested for use at the next session and effective only for that particular session, the fourth of the twenty fourth parliament. If the proposals are accepted now and tried out at the next session and found acceptable in practice, then of course the house may decide to incorporate them into the rules as a permanent feature.
The second reason for not dealing at great length with this particular subject is that the committee in its report is suggesting that a similar committee be set up early next session to carry on the studies which have already been started by the present committee, and to include the procedure on private bills of divorce, which the committee has been asked to consider and is willing to consider in so far as the problem is capable of procedural solution.
So we have before us the report of a committee on procedure which indicate that on this important subject there was no time for the committee to consider every phase of the rules and procedure of the house and bring in a complete report.
This follows the practice of other years. A committee which reported in 1955 was engaged in its activities of reviewing the rules for, I think, four sessions. To make an intensive study of the present rules of the house is something that cannot foe done in a few meetings; it must be spread over a considerable period of time. The committee

therefore is suggesting that a similar committee be established at the next session, and I hope it will be early enough in the next session for it to make a complete investigation. The rules of the House of Commons have been established over many years of trial and error, and are not lightly to be altered. However, as time goes on conditions change and it becomes apparent that some of the rules of the house might be altered in order to make it possible for members to deal more expeditiously with the business that comes before us.
It is interesting to review what has happened in former years with regard to alterations of the rules. In 1927 the rules of the house were changed in order to limit the time for speeches which prior to that were unlimited. The 40-minute rule for speeches was introduced following the session of 1927.
We had a number of changes in the rules suggested in 1955, and they have been operative up to the present. Some weaknesses in those changes have become apparent during the last few sessions, and to correct those or to suggest alternatives the committee has put forward certain proposals. These proposals may be carefully examined now, and of course it is open to hon. members to make other suggestions. In summary, the proposals are as follows.
The first proposal is to shorten the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne by two days. The rules now provide for 10 days, and the committee suggests that this be reduced to eight. The committee also proposes with respect to speeches during the course of that debate, with the exception of those by the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the mover of an amendment or a subamendment, other hon. members participating in the debate shall have 30 minutes available to them rather than the present 40 minutes. This is done so that with a reduction of two days in the over-all length of the debate there will still be an opportunity for as many hon. members to participate as is done normally when 10 days are available and 40 minutes per member.
The second proposal is somewhat similar and deals with the budget debate, which under the present rules has an over-all length of eight days. The suggestion put before us in the second proposal is that we shorten it by two days, to six in all, and that the same restriction be applicable that is applicable to the throne speech debate, with 30 minutes being given each hon. member who participates except the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, the Minister of Finance, the hon. member speaking on behalf of the opposition following the budget

address, and the mover of a subamendment who will be given 40 minutes. Those two proposals indicate that from the fixed debates which the present rules permit, four days would be taken off.
The third proposal is somewhat different. Under the present rules, after the address in reply to the speech from the throne is concluded the two next Thursdays are provided as private members' days, and the six Mondays succeeding the conclusion of the debate I have mentioned, unless those Mondays are interrupted by provision for supply motions. The result is that for a period of perhaps 10 or 11 weeks, on Monday and sometimes Thursday there is no opportunity to bring forward government business either by way of setting up committees or introducing legislation.
The suggestion now made is that some flexibility be permitted with regard to those private members' Mondays and Thursdays. The explanatory note in the report of the committee with respect to this proposal reads as follows:
In order to provide more time for government business in the early stage of the next session, the foregoing proposal provides machinery whereby private members' days may be deferred when so requested by a minister of the crown. No reduction is being proposed in the number of days now provided for private members' business.
The deferment amounts briefly to this. If in the opinion of the government, on one of the Mondays that would normally be a private members' day there is an opportunity to bring forward government business, that Monday be deferred for a week or two. The same applies to Thursday. The proposed change in the rules as to deferment is set out clearly but it is important to note that the two Thursdays and the six Mondays are retained so there is no reduction in the over-all time now provided under the rules for private members to bring various matters to the attention of the house.
The fourth proposal is quite simple. It suggests an alteration in standing order No. 15, which refers to the hour from five to six o'clock p.m. on Tuesdays and Fridays. The standing order now reads:
Private and public bills, the former having precedence.
The alteration would permit public bills to precede private bills on Friday. The result would be that on Tuesday the first item in the period from five to o'clock would be private bills and on Friday the order would be reversed and public bills would come in advance of private bills. We have found this year that this would have been helpful, in that certain public bills have either been brought forward by unanimous consent of
Procedure Committee
the house or perhaps have not come to the attention of the house. It appears to be rather more equitable to alternate those on Tuesdays and Fridays.
Those are the four proposals which have been put forward by your committee, Mr. Speaker, consisting of representatives of all three parties in the house. I might add that the committee's report is unanimous. The committee met on several occasions and of course would have continued its work had it thought it possible to do more than this in the course of this session, but having made a start the committee would like to see a similar committee appointed next year.
What can be accomplished by revision of the rules is open to serious consideration and, naturally, to question. Whether or not sessions can be reduced in length is something that a committee on rules must look into very carefully. Over the years innumerable suggestions have been made in this connection, but committees sitting on the question of rules and procedures have found it is not easy to determine the length of any session.
A few years ago I was interested in this subject, and took as a starting point the changes made in the rules in 1927. I put forward the proposition that if prior to 1927 hon. members were permitted to speak for an unlimited period of time-two hours, five hours, seven hours-and after 1927 they were restricted to speeches of 40 minutes, therefore it must follow that the sessions from 1927 on were greatly reduced in length from those that preceded 1927. But I did not find that to be the case from my study of the sessions from 1900 to 1955.
I found that one of the longest sessions in Canada's history, perhaps exceeded by the session of 1956 and possibly also by this session, was, I think, the session of 1903 or 1904, when the house met early in March and prorogued late in November. If you look at Hansard for that period you will find hon. members complaining about the lengthy speeches, the use of Hansard, understandably and normally protesting about being away from their families and constituencies for a great length of time, the farmers complaining about missing seed-time and harvest and sitting in Ottawa through a hot summer. Therefore what we are going through this year is perhaps no different from what has happened in the past. I just bring this forward to illustrate that it is an easy generalization to say that things can be changed by an alteration in the rules. It does not necessarily follow.
By way of conclusion, and to give some information to the house in case hon. members want to touch on these matters, up to Saturday, which was the 143rd day of this

Procedure Committee
session, the debates which are either fixed by the rules or which were allotted because of special circumstances took up 44 days. They are divided in this way. The speech from the throne, including the opening day and the day taken up by the mover and the seconder, took 12 days; the budget debate, eight days; the external affairs debate, which was requested, three days; one day on commonwealth relations; six private members' Mondays; three private members' Thursdays, because an extra day was given there on request. There were five supply motions introduced, each taking two days; then recently another supply motion, which took part of a day, so that 11 days were devoted to supply motions, making a total of 44.
On supply itself, we have had 10 days on supplementary estimates, of which two were taken for agriculture and eight for labour. This was earlier in the session. Three days were taken on interim supply. Estimates of the departments which we have been considering recently have taken the greater part of 38 days, giving a total of 51 days for supply and consideration of estimates. The government business on legislation has had the remainder of the time, amounting to 48 days.
I bring this report of the committee to the attention of the house, repeating that it is unanimous; that it is on a trial basis and is suggested for the next session of the house, at which time we hope that another committee will continue a more intensive study of the rules in order to suit the house to the convenience of hon. members without restricting in any way the freedom of speech on which this institution lives and thrives.
It matters not how much we may desire various changes, I think we have to keep in mind that freedom of discussion is essential in a democracy, and restrictions that are imposed should be only such as are agreed on among members so that freedom remains; because if we do not have freedom of speech in this chamber, I am afraid that we could not maintain democracy as we know it.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who had the opportunity of serving on this select committee which was appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the procedure of this house for the purpose of suggesting any changes which may be desired to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business, I feel it appropriate that I take a moment of the time of the house to indicate some views on this report.
First of all, I should like to make it clear that as far as I am concerned it was a very pleasant committee to have the opportunity of serving on. That was due, perhaps,

to the method of having the committee do its work. It was a small committee, and that makes a committee work much more efficiently, in my view, and is a much better arrangement all around. Of course, I acknowledge at once the method of chairing the committee, and I must say that I found the guiding of the committee most efficiently performed. Then there is another matter of great significance. The committee met in camera, and certainly in discussing technical matters of this sort it is a more satisfactory method than meeting in public.
The committee report itself is, I think it is fair to say, very simple. It puts forward suggestions for the approval of this house for changes to be tried at the next session only. The house can then decide after the trial whether they should be continued or otherwise. I emphasize the fact that the recommended changes are for one session only.
The first proposals, perhaps, do not have very great significance, because they provide for the participation of the same number of members as under existing rules in the throne speech and the budget debates. While it is true that the time is reduced by one-quarter-the time allotted to each member is reduced from 40 minutes to 30 minutes- that perhaps is not any hardship, because these are formal debates and there is an opportunity for preparing speeches. It should result, at least I hope it results, in better preparation of the speeches. I would hope that the next session will reveal that the 30-minute speeches well prepared contain more than the 40-minutes speeches less well prepared.
I do feel that a word should be said about proposal No. 3. It seems to me there is a criticism of the conduct of the business of the house that could be validly made, and it has been made many times during this session; namely that the government business was not brought forward and presented to the house early enough in the session to permit a thorough discussion of it, and the motions to set up committees were not brought forward early enough in the session to permit the committees to start their work immediately after the throne speech had been disposed of. Some committees were set up very late in the session. To the criticism of this the government has from time to time made the reply that the government had no opportunity to bring forward those motions earlier in the session; that the time allotted to the government in the early part of the session is so limited that they do not risk bringing forward those less urgent matters such as motions to set up committees. Invariably, it seems to me, in the last number of years, going back to most of the post-war years, at the start of each session there had been some legislation

that appeared to be of a very urgent nature; the government had to present it in the day or two each week allotted to the government, and they did not feel that it was proper to use that time to present to the house certain motions to set up committees and that sort of thing because they had no way of knowing how long the debates on those motions would take, and indeed they might have to wait another week or so, as the case might be, before proceeding with their legislation.
As far as I am concerned, I think there has been some validity in the criticism made of the government about its lateness in presenting legislation and in setting up committees. There has been the answer that they have been able to give at least in the early weeks in the session, in the first two months after the throne speech, that a disproportionate part of the time at that stage of the session was taken up by private members days. Well, this proposal is put forward in an effort to meet that problem. I think now the government will have an opportunity, immediately the throne speech has been disposed of and it has its vote of confidence, to present its program of legislation to the house so the bills may be given first reading. Then they will be in the possession of hon. members for examination for some time before they come on for debate on second reading. The committees will be set up early in the session, and they can start their work. I feel that is a wholly desirable thing, and I think it-

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt, but would the hon. gentleman allow a question?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has given a great deal of study to this matter, and is recognized for that study. I should like to ask him what the situation is, if he can tell the house without having to look up the details, in the United Kingdom. What has their experience been?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, I shall briefly outline that experience. I do not hold myself out as an authority; in fact I am quite frank to tell you that I am not an authority. If I may just continue my remarks before answering that question, I would say that it seems to me this proposal is worthy of the greatest attention. It will mean that at the next session the government will either have to present the motion to set up the committees and present its program to the house at an early stage in the session, or leave itself open to the criticism of the opposition for not having done so. I believe that is a wholly desirable position from the point of view of both the government and the opposition,
Procedure Committee
and one that should commend itself to the house. I believe this is the most important of all the proposals put forward by the committee.
In so far as the United Kingdom committees are concerned, my understanding of the situation is that the number of members serving on each of their committees is very much smaller than ours. This is the main characteristic. One of the other characteristics is that the committees very frequently meet in camera, and they do not publish their evidence from day to day. The evidence is frequently published and presented with their report, and that is the first time the evidence is made public. These are the three pronounced distinctions, as I understand them, between the committees of the House of Commons in the two countries.
It is not, perhaps, germane to this report because the report does not deal with it, but there is another situation in so far as our committees are concerned, and that is the very large number of members serving on each of the standing committees. I have always felt that should be changed and the number should be reduced, so that instead of having one member serving on a great number of committees there would be greater selectivity and a member would only serve on a small number of committees. Some of our standing committees have as many as 60 members, and it seems to me that is wholly unreasonable. This number represents almost one quarter of the total membership of the house. In my experience I have never observed anything that led me to the opinion that this contributed to the efficiency of the committees, but rather it has another effect altogether.
Since the Prime Minister has raised the matter, perhaps I might add one other thing. It seems to me the great multiplicity of committees we have sitting has tended toward members moving from one committee to another without following one as closely as that member would wish. This is a very real problem, a practical problem, that should be borne in mind. However, I did not intend to digress into the committee question. I merely wanted to deal with the other matter, the expectation of the house that the government would, when these new rules are in operation, provide for the setting up of the committees at the start of the session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman say what is the course followed in the United Kingdom with regard to the setting up of committees? Has he that information available without having to look it up?

Procedure Committee

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I cannot give the Prime Minister a proper and full answer to that question.
It is regrettable that there was not sufficient opportunity to go into a great many other changes in the rules that might have been considered. So far as I am concerned, as a member of the committee, it was wholly proper that we should have contented ourselves with those things to which we thought we could give sufficient attention to bring forward proposals to the house at this session, rather than trying to cover the whole rule book.
There is, of course, one thing that is well for all members to bear in mind in considering these matters, and that is that the mere setting of the rules does not govern the whole procedure of the house. There is the matter of the conduct of the government in the timing of the introduction of legislation, the sequence of legislation, the allocation of days of debate, and all that sort of thing. As I see it, this aspect of the matter cannot be fully covered by the rules, nor would it be proper to do so. There is a whole area that, correctly, must be the responsibility of the government in submitting its business to the house. The government must stand or fall on its record of how it has carried out its responsibilities in this respect. It would be quite wrong, in my view, to attempt to spell out all these details in the book of rules. I hope that in the years that lie ahead the house will never do that.
There is the recommendation that a similar committee be appointed early in the next session. I hope the Prime Minister will give an undertaking to set up such committee very early in the next session.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report of the special committee appointed to consider the procedure of the House of Commons is undoubtedly a very important piece of business, and it is now before us. However, in view of the fact that the recommendations are very concise, the explanations are very clear, and it is a unanimous report which, if accepted, will be on a trial basis for a period of one year, I do not intend to speak at any length at this time. My personal views, Mr. Speaker, can best be put forward in the manner in which I have expressed them on previous occasions.
We in this group view the House of Commons as 265 representatives of the people elected to a board of directors, a board which by the will of the people expressed in a democratic election has the responsibility and the right of policy-making for the nation, of making, rescinding or changing laws, imposing taxation and spending the people's [Mr. Diefenbaker.l
money. For these great purposes the parliamentary system has been devised. I have no hesitation in saying, as I have said many times outside this house, that in my estimation the parliamentary institution is the greatest instrument ever devised by man for solving man's problems and for carrying out the will of the majority of the people of the nation.
Because of its responsibility as an institution and the responsibility of those who are elected to carry out the purposes I have just mentioned, it is of the utmost importance that the rules, regulations and procedure be such that every member has the fullest guarantee of the right to participate in all business of the House of Commons; that every member, irrespective of party, government, opposition, or third party like ourselves, or an independent, has full freedom, right and protection in this regard.
However, Mr. Speaker, having said that I would also add that in the necessity of parliament at all times fighting for the maintenance of the rights and freedoms and the exercise of parliamentary authority, at the same time there must be a recognition that an individual must exercise a personal restraint. There must not be the possibility or permissibility of reducing the dignity, decorum, efficiency and purpose of parliament into a state of licence or a mockery. In other words, what I am trying to say is that for the maintenance of the function of parliament, for the guarantee of all rights to all members of parliament, if there cannot be personal restraint then we must have rules, regulations and standing orders in order to maintain the efficiency, dignity and decorum of parliament itself.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I have been as guilty as anybody else, and that is the reason I can speak this way. I think that very, very often speeches that should be made in 30 minutes take 40 minutes. Points that could be made in 10 minutes sometimes take 30 minutes, and perhaps many of us are guilty of that. Also, I am very much afraid that very often cabinet ministers take two or three hours and could do a damned sight better job in one hour.

However I am convinced that the unanimous recommendation of this committee, suggesting that we give a trial to a reduction of two days in the throne speech debate and two days in the budget debate, with the majority of speeches down from 40 minutes to 30 minutes, is one that is well worth while. I have no hesitation in saying I am almost certain that we can all come within those limitations; at least we will find out at the next session.

But I do think some of the changes recommended are of the utmost importance, changes that will give a greater guarantee of the appointment of committees at an earlier time of the session, the introduction of government business at an earlier time of the session, an opportunity of carrying out the people's business as it is seen from the government's point of view. Whether you like it or not, that is the point of view we have to start with, because they have the power. That will be adding to the greater efficiency of parliament itself.
Therefore, sir, I repeat that on the basis of the recommendation of the trial period, it is well worth while, and we should have the opportunity of seeing whether or not this can increase our efficiency without in any way restricting of rights of members of parliament. We should adopt this report and proceed next session as recommended.
Of course, sir, I do want to add a word on the last section of the report:
It is therefore recommended that a similar committee he appointed early in the next session to carry on these studies including the procedure on private bills of divorce which the committee has been asked and is willing to consider in so far as the problem is capable of procedural solution.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a most important and worth-while recommendation. Over the years many of us have been worried about the procedure of parliament, both in this house and the other place, whereby both have to sit as a court and handle divorce proceedings from two provinces. Of course, sir, a solution has got to be found, or consideration given not just to procedural matters but to the entire question of the divorce laws of this country, to modernizing them and getting away from the antiquated divorce laws with which our country is cursed.
However, sir, the procedural committee has not the authority to deal with that phase. At this session the insanity of the present procedure has been made obvious. Two members, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters), have I think done a service to this country in focusing attention on the antiquity and insanity of our present procedure. Perhaps nothing can be done at this session, but I want to commend the committee that has been dealing with the standing orders and parliamentary procedure in that they have unanimously recommended to this house that the committee be reconvened early next session, when it will consider not only the many other matters of importance concerning the business of this house, but will give consideration to divorce procedure as well.
I am convinced, sir, that if this recommendation is accepted we can look forward 79951-0-490
Procedure Committee
next year to real consideration being given by all members of that committee to a most serious and complicated problem. I know they will eventually come up-I hope unan-inously-with a recommendation that will meet with the approbation of the House of Commons and of the other place, so as to remove this iniquitous problem from within the purview of the other place and the House of Commons.
Therefore, sir, in conclusion I say that we believe it is quite conceivable, and most possible, that the acceptance of the report now before us by this committee of a trial period next year, with the further consideration of these and other matters by the early reappointment of the committee, can only prove of benefit to this house, and gives an indication right now of the seriousness with which all members view their responsibility as to the integrity, the decorum and the efficiency of parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by confirming and agreeing with the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West concerning the chairmanship of the committee and the rather unique manner in which our meetings were conducted, I suspect out of lack of other times during the day, within the lunch or dinner hour. It certainly seemed to me a most appropriate way to proceed.
I am going to have to watch the clock very carefully, Mr. Speaker. I propose to say something about the virtues of a 15-minute speech, and I think it would be most inappropriate if, after making what I hope is a case for such a proposition, I should go beyond that period.
I noticed with considerable interest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when introducing the debate on this subject, stated that one of the overriding considerations in reducing the number of days of debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne was that it was felt the same number of members would participate as has been the case in previous years. I had the figures looked up of the number of speakers who participated in the throne speech debate over the last few years, and I would like to put these figures on record. They are as follows:

This averages out over the period to approximately 102 members a year.
One of the suggestions I would like to put on the record at this time for the future consideration of the committee, both with regard to the speech from the throne and the budget debate, is that a certain number of days during those debates be set aside for 15-minute speeches. I have done some very rough arithmetic, and if, say, three of the eight days were restricted to 15-minute speeches, at least 100 and at most about 195 members could participate in the throne speech debate, and a proportionately less number could participate in the budget debate. I think that is a very important and a very desirable end in itself.
I would also like to see portions of other debates allocated on the same basis. We could take, out of a two-day supply motion, two or three hours and restrict contributions at that stage of the debate to 15-minute speeches. This could also apply to certain of the private members' days, and I think would contribute toward more effective debate. I also think that in restricting the length of a speech it might produce the result that there would be more of what is described as the cut and thrust of debate, with a larger number of members interested in the development of the theme of the debate.
I have in this connection examined various debates held in the British House of Commons, and I have found that one speaker will bring forward a point, the speaker following him will knock it down, the next speaker will support the first speaker and prop it up again, and so the battle goes on back and forth like a ball in a tennis match, resulting in both interesting reading and I am sure very good listening as well.
It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that a 15-minute speech or a short speech is a far more difficult speech to prepare, and I would suggest rather more difficult to deliver effectively. I think the greatest merit in a 15-minute speech as far as most subjects are concerned is that you end up by rejecting certain points and selecting only salient points which you wish to include in your speech, instead of making a 40-minute or even longer speech covering everything even remotely connected with your subject. I think the very selection of your material to include into a short speech inevitably makes it more pointed and better.
I have had discussions with newspapermen and particularly with columnists who have small space to fill each day in their paper, and to a man they all agree that it is far more difficult to write a short column. I was always greatly impressed by some columnists who could fill a long column in a newspaper every day and yet keep it interesting. I have

found, as I have said, that this presents no real challenge, that it is not difficult to keep talking but is sometimes very difficult to stop talking. And as I say, Mr. Speaker, I am keeping a very close watch on my time at this moment.
There are occasions under the English procedure where speechs are limited to ten minutes; but I would like to leave that with the committee as one of my suggestions. I think it would contribute to wider participation and should be adopted on some future occasion on a trial basis. I also think this parliament and this government, with its extended use of committees, has demonstrated that there can be more effective contribution made by the backbenchers, and this has been shown in my view to be beyond any doubt. I think certain periods of days, three in the throne speech debate and possibly two in the budget debate, limited to 15-minute speeches would produce much more effective speeches and wider and more effective contributions.
The last point I would like to make before resuming my seat is to suggest that notices of motions or resolutions be given a better break in the scheme of things than they have hitherto. Very early in the session the resolutions disappear from the order paper and there is no further opportunity to debate them, though some of them are very provocative items indeed. I suggest that one hour a month, alternatively on Tuesdays and Fridays, be devoted to a continuation of the discussion of these notices of motions and resolutions.
Mr. Speaker, I think that brings me fairly close to a 15-minute speech, so I will resume my seat at this point.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having in mind the remarks of the hon. member who has just preceded me, I shall also endeavour to keep my remarks fairly short. I think basically the object of the report which is before the House of Commons is to keep in mind the fact that usually the listener tires much more quickly than the speaker does. I notice in the report that it is indicated that this is a temporary report, or at least that the recommendations on procedure be adopted on a trial basis effective only for the next session of parliament.
Recently I read in the newspapers, and no doubt, Mr. Speaker, you have too, that there is a possibility of a fall session. Having this newspaper speculation in mind, I suggest that this would be the time to give serious consideration to the temporary measures you have suggested, and further to give effect to the suggestion that the seats in the House of Commons be removed, as is done at the end of each session, and be replaced if we

have a fall session, with benches in an effort to try out the practice adopted in the United Kingdom house.
I feel that the only way we can get a change in the rules is to create a psychological impact and also to have a change in environment, and I think this would be perhaps one of the most effective ways of doing it. Having benches replace the present seats would not put speakers like myself sitting off at the side at a bolted desk. You would also have a tendency to shorter speeches limited to notes which could be held in the hand or contributed from memory.
In addition, this would put speakers much closer to the Hansard reporter, where they could congregate together. I feel I am at a considerable disadvantage because of my position in the house when I want to raise an objection. All the front benchers on both sides of the house are fairly close to the Hansard reporter and are able to get in what at times are very damaging remarks. That is why I feel that a person like myself off at the side is to a certain extent discriminated against. Although some interjections are of the humorous kind, some of the hon. members over on the side near the Hansard reporter can interject some remark which I do not hear and therefore cannot reply to, yet it is reported and appears in the printed publication, whereas I would have replied had I heard it.
I also feel that having the seats replaced with benches would have the effect of making the criss-cross of debate much more rapid. This will have the effect of making crisscross debate much more accurate and more rapid. As a new member of parliament I find that perhaps the most interesting part of parliament is the question period, and when visitors come here I advise them to attend during the question period because that is the time when there is a fast exchange of ideas and when the proceedings are more akin to a debate of the type one might expect.
Speaking again as a new member, if I had any advice to give to others coming into parliament I would say that with respect to the rules there are only two basic things you need to know. If you wish to get on your feet and talk, regardless of the subject matter under discussion, the first thing to learn to say is: "Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order". Then you stand up and make whatever observation you desire to make. The speaker then draws to your attention the fact that the point of order you raised is really not a point of order and that it does not concern the matter which is before the house. Nevertheless, you have succeeded in getting in your interjection. The other alternative is to say: "Mr. Speaker, I 79951-0-490i
Procedure Committee
rise on a question of privilege." That stops everything. You stand up to deal with your question of privilege and you preface it by a few remarks. Then, ultimately, you come to the question of privilege itself. Since I have been in this house one of the things which has impressed me is the number of times a point of order has been ruled not to be a point of order and a question of privilege not to be a question of privilege. I realize that this is perhaps one of the most difficult problems facing the occupant of the speaker's chair, because by the time the ruling is made whatever has been said is already on the record. But this does underline the importance of knowing the rules and of a healthy discipline among members of parliament themselves.
On this whole matter of a knowledge of the rules-and here again I can only speak as a new member-we are given a basic idea of what the rules are by our parties and then we are handed a large edition of Beauchesne. After that we take our seats in the House of Commons. I feel that serious consideration should be given to setting up a nonpartisan instruction committee on the rules of the house, because it has struck me that on a great many occasions more time has been spent here in discussing the rules, and the effect that can be given to them, than the business itself.
Another suggestion which we might consider is that all members of parliament should sit for an examination at the end of which they must receive a mark of at least 50 per cent. In the province of British Columbia even our drivers have to pass a test as to their ability before they are allowed on the road, but a member of parliament can be turned loose on one of the most expensive roads in the country, metaphorically speaking, without anyone knowing whether he is familiar with any of the rules. In answer to a question which was asked in the house, as reported in Hansard on July 1, 1955, it was estimated that it cost $5,070,235 a session to run parliament. That works out at a cost of something like $17,377 per day and when we consider that a session can be prolonged by a misunderstanding of the rules I think the proposal I have put forward is not too much to suggest, namely that this committee should be set up so that not only is the Speaker aware of the rules but that hon. members may have an understanding of them as well.
If I may make one word of criticism, it is this: I think the older members of parliament who should be setting the standards for the new members have been among the worst offenders in incurring reprimands on

Procedure Committee
questions of order. I think they should take a close look at their own practices and attempt to set a standard which other members such as myself could imitate. I feel that no matter how we try to improve the rules a tremendous amount must depend on the self-discipline of individuals, and we new members of parliament look to the senior members to set the standard. By raising points of order which are not points of order and questions of privilege which are ruled not to be questions of privilege I suggest they are doing a great deal of damage. I understand that it was said of the late Mr. Arthur Meighen that never during his career did he have to be ruled out of order by the speaker.
Another suggestion I have to make is that a loose leaf rule book be prepared containing every rule likely to be encountered printed on a separate page with a comment on the origin and purpose of the particular rule. I suggest, also, that the Speaker's rulings as reported in Votes and Proceedings should also be put in loose leaf form and made available and then each member could have before him up to date rules together with the latest rulings so that he would not be at a disadvantage compared with those who were a little more careful in trying to get some background information.
There are one or two other matters I should like to raise in connection with saving the time of parliament and the first concerns the question of an electrical system of recording votes. I raised this question as a grievance on February 10, 1959 because it seems to me it is a considerable waste of time to spend almost half an hour in getting a vote. I think I would still be in favour of having the first vote of a session a standing vote but I believe that subsequent votes should be recorded by the use of an electronic system. I became interested in this matter through an article in the Christian Science Monitor dealing with the use of such machines in Connecticut and the likelihood of their introduction into the state of Massachusetts. Having read that article I thought that perhaps this would be the solution to our own problem and I wrote to the International Roll-Call Corporation. In reply, I received the following letter dated June 20, 1959. It reads:
Thank you for your letter of May 29. We are enclosing literature.
Thirty two of the 33 electrical roll call systems In use in our legislatures are our machines, and the other is a copy. Our latest model is in 15 of these assemblies. The largest, in Hartford, Connecticut, is the size you require: a 300 member machine with 279 actual members.
[Mr. Drysdale.l
Possibly you or a committee could see this machine in Hartford. We also have a 40-member demonstrator, that we can send by truck to interested legislatures.
The Connecticut machine was installed under a rental and maintenance contract, for $35,000 on the first year, and $10,000 and $15,000. We cannot give exact figures without inspecting the building. The Connecticut contract has a purchase option in it for $175,000 less rentals paid, which was not exercised. Such purchase options seldom are exercised, because in a field as small as this rental with company maintenance seems to be the best arrangement. If such an option was carried in your contract it would no doubt exceed $200,000, and it could make it difficult to get the legislation through. We think a straight rental and maintenance contract is the easiest to have adopted, and the best for both parties, unless there is some specific reason demanding purchase.
The machine in Connecticut records the vote on a perforated card, in triplicate, in 10 to 15 seconds. Any number of duplicate records also can be made. The indicator boards can be kept illuminated or dark while the vote is recorded. Some states display the totals continuously while the members are voting, with the latest totals appearing every six to ten seconds depending on size of the machine. No state ever has given up electrical voting after having once used it.
I was very fortunate in obtaining the co-operation of this company, which has its main office in Richmond, Virginia, in having them send up the demonstrator unit to allow hon. members of parliament and others interested in the procedure to see the machine work at first hand. I received some criticism from some hon. members about the fact that this machine is manufactured by a United States firm. I should like to draw to the attention of the house the fact that these machines are rather unusual. This was the only company I knew of in the United States that manufactured these machines and I do not believe any companies in Canada make such units although I believe it would be possible to have one made here.
I noticed the reference of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to his having seen a similar machine in India. I was advised by the people who make this machine that the one in use in India was based on their unit. The people from India came to view their machine and upon returning to India designed a similar one for their own use. I have put forward this information about the machine with the thought in mind that should it be favourably considered by parliament it could be decided to have a Canadian company design and make such a machine.
With regard to the House of Commons itself I would envisage the tabulator boards being placed on the panels above the clocks bn each side of the house. It would be necessary to have the 265 names on the board. At each desk there would be a toggle type switch similar to a light switch which would record a yea and nay vote.

One of the first questions I had asked me was what is to prevent a person sitting in the seat beside you from reaching over and recording a vote. I suggest that we would have to do what was done in various state legislatures, pass legislation making it an offence to do that. There would also be the check of the board being visible with lights in red or white indicating a yea or nay vote. Each person would be in a position when a vote was recorded to see whether or not an hon. member was in his seat.
One other advantage of this particular type of machine is that there is a switch which calls for page service. This is accomplished by having a board with numbers corresponding to the various seats in the chamber with a light for each seat. The panel could be located in the lobby. By pressing a switch any hon. member requiring a page could have a page come silently to his desk without the usual finger snapping that is necessary to bring a page to us under our present system.
As I said the machine can register a vote in some 15 to 30 seconds. It think it would be of particular value in the committee stage of the proceedings, for example on a bill such as the bill of rights when the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) introduced innumerable amendments. There would be a considerable saving of time through the use of a machine that could handle a vote in 10 or 15 seconds rather than the three or four minutes required by a standing vote. It would enable us to bring in more amendments and dispose of them much more quickly.
One rather humorous aspect in connection with the machine that was drawn to my attention is that the machine is put in operation in the various state legislatures by the speaker of the legislature activating a switch which rings a gong. I was advised that in the state of Maryland which is noted for its horse racing whenever the gong rings the majority of the people in the legislature immediately shout "They're off!" which lends a humorous note to the proceedings.
I have attempted in my comments with respect to the procedure to draw to the attention of the house my own views as a relatively new member of parliament. I realize that I have not had the experience of many years here and there may be readily discernible faults in some of the remarks I have made. I appreciate the necessity for old age, maturity and experience in examining certain matters but a new member coming to this house has an opportunity to examine the procedures and ask why this or that is
Procedure Committee
being done, or why there is a necessity lor continuing this or that practice.
One matter that has come to my attention is this. I observe that under rule No. 28 I would have to remove my hat, if I were wearing one, before I could rise to address you, Mr. Speaker. I realize that in the early days because of drafts in the chamber hon. members might well have worn hats while in the house and this was perhaps a necessary rule but in this enlightened period of air conditioning and central heating such a rule remains as a humourous anachronism. That is an example of a rule that should be changed.
