speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting
and perhaps not inappropriate that we should be discussing this report designed to improve our procedures on the 144th day of our session after Hansard has broken all records in the number of pages that have been filled. As has been said by other hon. members it is a useful report, one unanimously brought in by the committee and I hope it will win the unanimous support of the house.
Our rules and procedures are designed for many purposes, to minister to the efficiency and the order of our business, to make parliament function as effectively as is possible and also-and this is an important purpose
to protect the rights of the minority in the house as well as to facilitate the business of the house.
In the 1956-57 issue of the Queen's Quarterly, volume LXIII, there were some very interesting articles on parliamentary procedure including one by Your Honour which I should like to quote but perhaps I should not. There was also one by a man who over the years in this house established himself as a recognized expert on our rules and procedures, Mr. Stanley Knowles. Mr. Knowles had this to say:
It is-important, as Bourinot puts it, "to protect a minority and restrain the improvidence or tyranny of a majority,-to enable every member to express his opinion-to give abundant opportunity for the consideration of every measure, and to prevent any legislative action being taken upon sudden impulse."

Procedure Committee
That concludes the quotation from Bouri-not. Mr. Knowles went on to say:
That is the problem that faces anyone who would seek to improve our parliamentary procedure: to maintain a balance between getting the business of the country done and protecting the rights of those who have been chosen by the citizens of the country to speak for them in relation to that business.
It is the reconciliation that Mr. Knowles talks about we are all anxious to achieve. This report makes some recommendations which I think will be useful to that end. It seems to me the changes are very sensible ones as far as they go but perhaps something more far-reaching is required not only in connection with our rules but in connection with our conduct of business if we are to make our parliamentary procedures work more efficiently as we all want to do as parliament faces new, more difficult and increasingly complicated problems. 1 believe we all want to do that without destroying or weakening the traditions of parliament which are our heritage and which we wish to preserve, especially the spirit of those traditions.
When parliament does not operate effectively that leads to the loss of public confidence in and public respect for our parliamentary institutions. This erosion, if you like, of confidence and prestige is, 1 submit, a greater danger to our institutions than direct assault upon them. The feeling -and there seems to be a growing feeling although it goes up and down; at the moment it seems to be going up-that we are not doing our work efficiently; that as an institution we are not meeting in the most effective way the problems that confront us; that our parliamentary business is not well managed. All this does undoubtedly lead to that deterioration of public confidence in parliament which we all, whatever party we may belong to, wish to avoid. We all have our share of responsibility for this. I think the government has the major share of responsibility because it has, up to a point at least, control of business and organization, but we all certainly do have our share. Also the rules under which we operate share in that responsibility, and that is why it is wise from time to time that we should look at them, as we have done this session.
As the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) pointed out, in 1955 an examination was made of the procedure of the house, which had not been seriously altered since 1880, although changes have been made since then. The minister pointed out that another change was made in 1927, which was the first time that a time limit was placed on speeches.

In 1955 the government of that day had hoped to make more far reaching proposals for change than were in fact submitted to parliament but there was difficulty, as some hon. members who sat on that committee will recall, in getting unanimous agreement to those changes, and it was felt then that the government should not use its majority to force those changes any more than the government has attempted to use its majority for that purpose in the work of this particular committee. In 1955 I think it can be said that only relatively minor changes were made. The changes that we have before us are, while useful, perhaps not of major importance in altering our procedures and our rules.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made a statement on this matter on July 21, on which he anticipated some of the provisions of this report and made some comments on some of the recommendations. He mentioned that in his view we were spending too much time on questions. I do not want to be unfair to him; perhaps he would say on the wrong kind of questions. I have what he said in Hansard on that date. He said that the extra time which was now devoted to questions, although he did not precisely define, because it is difficult indeed to precisely define, what he meant by "extra"-extra from what, but the extra time-the Prime Minister thought had added 14 to 17 days to the present session at that date. I would be interested to ascertain from the Prime Minister the nature of his mathematical calculations which he got from the extra time devoted to questions at this session to total 14 to 17 extra days. Perhaps our question period has begun to exceed the length of previous years, although I am not so sure of that, but I would not think that it had reached any excess, at least to that extent.
I agree there is something to be said-and I speak as a member of the opposition; the opposition are always very sensitive and jealous of their right to ask questions on anything, always subject to the Speaker's guidance; my hon. friends opposite will know what I mean when I say that-for the British practice of putting a limit on the kind of questions that can be asked orally. I welcome the announcement that there is to be a committee next session and I repeat what has been said on this side. It is our hope that that committee can be set up early and that it can be given lots of time and lots of opportunity to go into this whole thing from its foundation and return what will be the kind of unanimous report which we have before us.
Perhaps this is one of the things that they can look into when they go into procedure,

If our questions are becoming too long, so are some of our answers. A long question sometimes produces a short answer and a short question sometimes produces a long answer. While the opposition may have to accept its share of responsibility for this, and we do, the government must also share some of the responsibility by giving answers to questions which on this side do not appear as spontaneous as ours, and answers to questions which are used for the purpose of enunciating government policy sometimes and matters of policy. The Prime Minister will forgive me if I refer to the question the other day on the automobile industry which brought the announcement that a royal commission was going to be set up. Now, our question period may be deteriorating in other respects than length of time, and perhaps we all have some responsibility for that. This is something I am sure which the committee, on which all parties will be represented, would be glad to look into.
When the Prime Minister indicated that in his view this deterioration in some respects was taking place in the question period I looked up the record and I found that a couple of days after the Prime Minister's statement, on July 27 and 28, there were 12 questions from government members of parliament and only 13 from the opposition. I hasten to add that that is not a normal situation. But questions do come from all sides of the house and we all bear our share of the responsibility for the length of questions, if they should be carried on at an inordinate length.
The Prime Minister also made the statement, as reported at page 6673 of Hansard, that we should be careful about complaining too much about being overworked, the length of the session and that kind of thing. I agree with that. I suppose that parliaments from 1867 on have got themselves at one time or another into a position where they complained about overwork, managing the session, the length of speeches, and all the rest of it, sitting into the hot weather and not getting home; but the Prime Minister supported that statement by saying that they had much longer sittings in the United Kingdom where each session, he told us, was approximately 200 parliamentary days. I was surprised at that and perhaps the Prime Minister may not have meant to use that figure.

speechtext:
I will quote what the Prime Minister said:
In so far as the United Kingdom is concerned, that parliament sits in each session for approximately 200 parliamentary days.
Procedure Committee
This may well be our longest session. I do not think we have reached the record yet. We have sat only 144 days and if those two figures are right, we certainly have no cause for complaint. I checked the record again and I found that in 1959 the United Kingdom parliament sat for only 142 days, and so far this year it has sat for only 116 days. But in any event, I think we can learn a good deal from United Kingdom procedures. We have in the past, and I think we can in the future. While we do not wish to copy everything that is done by Westminster, they have had a great deal of experience and we can adopt some of their changes in recent years to our own situation. Perhaps we can make some progress in that direction.
Surely what is required is that without abandoning or weakening our traditional practices and procedures we could strive to improve and recast them, if necessary, in the interests of the efficient organization of the business of parliament, and for that the cooperation of everybody in the House of Commons is required. Above all in this respect, and this has been mentioned previously in this discussion, it is of primary importance to plan the work of the House of Commons and to organize that work, if possible by agreement, the kind of agreement which is now customary. Like so many things that are customary in the United Kingdom, it is almost more effective than if it were written. In the United Kingdom, the time to be allocated to important features of legislation is worked out in an informal way, of course with the knowledge and consent of the Speaker who, I believe, can overrule these informal agreements if he so wishes. Perhaps this would be worth looking into, as a way in which we could improve our procedure for the conduct of debates in this house.
Then, of course, a good deal has been said, and a good deal should be said, about the use of committees, committees not merely for partisan witchhunting on either side, committees not merely to get the government out of difficulties or to assist the opposition in creating difficulties for the government, but committees which would take some of the burden off the House of Commons as a whole without prejudicing or preventing in any way the full participation of all members in the House of Commons itself. We could gain something by a further look at the United Kingdom practice in this regard. The Prime Minister asked a question a few moments ago about the United Kingdom committees, and it is my impression that certainly some of the standing committees are set up at the beginning of the session. It

Procedure Committee
is surely important that we try to do that in this House of Commons. If our rules and procedures make that now impossible, and I know there are some difficulties in that regard under our present rules, we could change those rules for that particular purpose to get our committees started early. We could take all the necessary steps to change our rules to make that possible.
Then there is something else-in fact, there are a great many other things which I am not going to mention-and I mention this with some diffidence as it would be a great break with tradition. Perhaps before I come to that I should express my most hearty agreement with the suggestions that have just been made about improving our voting facilities. I do not see why it is any reflection on the democratic process if we are recorded in one way or in another way, provided we are recorded. There are ways of doing this, whether you stand and are counted or whether you are counted without standing, and so long as the principle of an individual record is maintained I would hope we could reduce the 10 or 15 minutes required for that purpose.
I believe there will be agreement that over recent years there has been an assimilation, if that is the right word, of the debate at the resolution stage of the bill to that of second reading which was never meant to take place and which, in earlier days, I do not think did take place. There is a historic reason for the resolution stage of any bill involving public expenditures and it goes back to the 17th century when the crown had control of the purse. This was a way of ensuring that control would come under common scrutiny. This particular justification for the resolution stage in the debate no longer exists. There are other justifications, but if we are to maintain these two stages I think we should look into the process of debate in each stage, and at least examine into the possibility of having merely one debate instead of two. Perhaps this would be going too far, but at least it could be examined. I will conclude, Mr. Speaker, merely by expressing my support for those changes that are suggested, and my strong support for a further, perhaps more complete examination of our rules and procedures by a committee next year than this committee was able to give for reasons which had nothing to do with the competence of the committee and certainly nothing to do with the competence of the chairman. Tribute has already been paid to him, and I think tribute should be paid to the committee as well. We who believe in parliament, we who love parliament, and that includes us all, whether we are on the government side or
tMr. Pearson.]
on the opposition side, are all concerned with making parliament the most effective agency possible for meeting the problems which are facing it now and will face it in the future. We have had some very good illustrations of this problem of the importance of organization at the procedural level in this session. If we do that, we can not only make our work here more effective but we can strengthen the prestige and the good name of parliamentary institutions themselves.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As a new member I hesitate to take part in this debate on this motion regarding the rules of the house. I have only one comment to make at this time, and that is with regard to the growing practice of members who are speaking to continue their remarks even when Mr. Speaker has risen to call order. I mention no particular member, but I can see a few offenders in this regard. The chief offender is not present. I should like to suggest to the committee on procedure which will be set up next session that a recommendation be made to the effect that when you rise, Mr. Speaker, the Hansard reporter immediately cease to report the words of the person speaking. I believe this would end many of the comments which now appear on Hansard after you have called order.
I hope that this suggestion will be considered by the next committee on rules and procedures. I might say that the present practice of continuing to speak after Mr. Speaker has risen has been drawn to my attention with very caustic comments by visitors in the gallery.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have waited to make my remarks on this report until most of the members who may wish to speak on other parts of the report have spoken. I want to refer to only one paragraph near the end of the report, and I hope to confine my remarks to that paragraph. The report of the committee includes this paragraph:
It is therefore recommended that a similar committee be appointed early in the next session to carry on these studies including the procedure on private bills of divorce which the committee has been asked and is willing to consider in so far as the problem is capable of procedural solution.
We are very pleased that the committee had the courage and took the opportunity of making this recommendation. It seems to me that after its consideration the committee will find that very little is to be gained from considering the matter from its procedural aspects.
However, this was necessary. It is necessary for parliament itself to admit that there is a problem in handling divorces in parliament,

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
and I am sure that when it examines the situation the committee will come up with the recommendation that a larger committee has to be established which will take in the other house as well as this house in the deliberation as to what will be the final solution regarding this matter of divorce.
We concur in the report in so far as they are willing to discuss this matter and to give consideration to the procedure. I hope, and I am sure, that they will not come up with only a solution of eliminating the opportunity of debate on private bills of divorce, but will come up with a solution that will say that private bills of divorce are not the same type of bills as other private bills sponsored through parliament.
This problem of handling divorce in parliament is not unique to Canada. The same problems have arisen in Europe. They have been predominant in the British parliament, and it is not many years ago that the matter was debated there and conclusions arrived at, when they eliminated some of the problems as they affected the senior parliament in England.
I would recommend to those who are interested in the changes that have been made in England that they read a small novel written by A. P. Herbert called "Holy Deadlock". He wrote this small book, which is a take-off on divorce procedures in that country. It points out the amusing situations that people in Canada get into when they try to get a divorce. I think members would not only be amused in reading this; they would also come to the conclusion that the British people came to, that it was not enough to make a mockery of parliament, but that something had to be done about it. He was subsequently elected to parliament and the divorce laws they have now were introduced.
This problem has also been a problem in all the commonwealth countries. Australia has done something about it in the last two years. New Zealand has given consideration to the problem. It has been discussed in Canada over the years, and we can go back to the years of J. S. Woodsworth when he discussed this matter in the House of Commons. He was shocked with the things that were happening then in relation to divorce. He continuously pestered the government of the day, and Mr. King finally said, "If you will get the province of Ontario to petition us, we will be glad to set up a court in that province". I think public opinion, and probably not Mr. Woodsworth, was responsible for the petition being presented, and subsequently divorce courts were established in the province of Ontario.
Mr. Pallet!: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member indicate the year of this petition to which he refers?
Procedure Committee

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The petition was presented, I believe, in 1928 and 1929, and the divorce courts in the province of Ontario were set up in 1930.
The debates in parliament indicate that this was a very pertinent matter in 1928. Mr. Coldwell, Mr. Knowles and other members of the C.C.F. party, as well as many other members of parliament, have over the years spoken of the problems, the disgusting problem that faces parliament when it has to discuss these things on which it has to pass judgment, things they are not completely fimiliar with and that in the main they do not want to have anything to do with.
Mr. Speaker, when I was first elected to the House of Commons the first experience I had in knowing that we were going to have to discuss and have some consideration for legal matters was the Terry case. In that case, as I remember it, the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) and I were both shocked with the fact that the woman in that case, if the divorce was granted, could be under the laws of the province of Quebec-[DOT] over which we had no authority-left completely destitute, although it was pointed out that she had put a large sum of money into a company and this company over the years had developed into something worth while.
Mr. Speaker, we spoke on that particular case long enough that it did not pass parliament. It returned to the Senate the next year, and they did not see fit to pass it for the second time. It was reintroduced, I believe, this year and no consideration was given to it.
A divorce is granted in parliament in quite a simple way. People from those provinces who have not the right of redress in their own provinces can come to the federal government, because the British North America Act gives the federal government the right to rule on marriage and divorce. They can come to parliament and petition for relief for any reason they wish. The one that most of them appeal on is relief from a marriage to the other party.
This year 609 applications were made to the Senate divorce committee. Each one cost $210 for the application. This amounted to $127,890. Of these, 492 cases were heard and passed; seven were turned down for lack of evidence as to adultery; 15 were withdrawn; 95 were not ready to be heard at the current session; 12 were contested before the Senate committee.
The Senate committee operates in a manner similar to a court. They have rules which they set for themselves and they have decided on what grounds the divorce action will be accepted. They are composed of a central committee, with three subcommittees, each

Procedure Committee
having three members. So it is not very difficult to ascertain how much time is taken up in the Senate on the matter of handling divorce actions.
The House of Commons, on the other hand, gives consideration to these bills in the form of first and second reading. They have the opportunity of going before a committee of the house and returned for third reading. They then only obtain a decree absolute when the Governor General gives royal assent.
Some of the problems that we are faced with, in my opinion, are these. The committee is not a court, despite legal advice to the contrary. Power on Divorce, in the fourth supplement, points out on page 35, under section 22 dealing with parliamentary divorce in general:
The Senate's committee on divorce is not a court of justice: its report is not a judgment.
This resulted from the case of Coorsh versus Decker (1956) Quebec, Canadian Current Law, 1038. Mr. Speaker, if it were a court of law, many of the things that happen in that committee would not be allowed to happen. We in the House of Commons, and particularly our chairman, have patterned our action on the action of our counterpart in the Senate. I believe that while the Senate has operated to the best of its ability and has set up a procedure of certain rights and certain conditions, the House of Commons in its committee has never set up a set of rules and does not operate according to any particular procedure.
The committee itself has no competent legal advice. It has the use of the house lawyers, and certainly it has a great deal of free advice from lawyers on that committee. But there is no particular legal advice that is worthy of consideration as far as the committee itself is concerned.
It is true that there has been advice given by the house lawyers as to jurisdiction and constitutional problems, but the ordinary jurisprudence that would be decided by a judge is, in my opinion, lacking in this committee. The committee has no power to call witnesses. This has been a problem that has caused a great deal of difficulty for the last year or so. The advice in the past from those who were consulted was that this committee did not have that right because it was a private bill; it was asking for information on private matters.
Mr. Speaker, I would point out that in my opinion this advice is wrong. This committee has the same rights as any other committee and I refer you to page 1098 of Hansard for February 16 of this year where various standing committees were set up, including the miscellaneous private bills committee. At page

1099 under the heading "Powers of committees", the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved:
That the standing committees of this house be severally empowered to examine and inquire into all such matters and things as may be referred to them by the house, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, with power to send for persons, papers and records.
I think we have had this power for some time, but I also think we have never exercised it and on many occasion have been advised that we did not have that power. Therefore many people who have been brought before this committee have been unable to prove their case because they did not have the right to subpoena witnesses and bring reluctant and at the same time hostile witnesses before the committee.
Would the hon. member permit a question. Who has asked for that right?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is true, but I think that whenever they phoned the clerk they have been given that advice and therefore did not appear before the committee and ask for that power. I think it was assumed by the clerks of the committee that they did not have the right to make this type of application.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The chairman of the committee says nonsense. I think frankly the whole committee has been nonsense and I include in that some of the actions of its chairman, who has set himself up in the position sometimes as judge as well as part of the jury.
In some cases where perjury is being committed, where one party testifies to a fact and the other party contradicts it, I think it would be to the advantage of the public to have the right to investigate and call witnesses to prove perjury was committed and to arrive at some decision about it.
Another problem with this particular committee of the House of Commons has been that the jury itself keeps changing. A juror will come in at the last moment prepared to decide a case he has not heard at all, and those jurors who have sat there and heard the case will get up at the last moment and leave.
You do it all the time, the two of you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I think another problem is this matter of never being able to investigate the charges which have been made, and I would like to refer to a case of a year or so ago when one of the corespondents showed statements from gas station operators to the effect that he had been in another town and

it was quite within the realm of impossibility for him to be where he was supposed to have been if only he could have proved it. I think in that particular case we should have had the right as a committee to investigate to find out if that was true or not.
One of the biggest problems affecting the whole operation of parliamentary divorce is this matter of our lack of jurisdiction in relation to children. We have continually been brought to task for mentioning the children, yet every law on the statute books of almost every country as far as I know has given predominance to the welfare of children in the matter of divorce. Those countries have always bent over backwards to see that the religion, the welfare, the stability and the education of those children was given paramount consideration. Yet we pass divorces in Canada where we have not the right to say that the children will receive any type of protection or settlement at all. We have given no protection to a wife who is framed, which I think has been the case in several cases, and in particular I refer to the Terry case.
There is another grave failure with this committee, and it is only one of many, and that is the fact that these divorces are granted in the main to people living in the province of Quebec, yet very few Quebec members ever sit on the committee or take any part in deciding what should be done with cases arising from their province. It seems to me that many of them have shirked their duties in refusing or not accepting the responsibility of sitting on the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member is going a little beyond the scope of relevancy here.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last but by no means least is the fact that these divorces are very expensive and only apply to those people who are in the well-off bracket or are fairly wealthy. It is estimated that a divorce costs anywhere from $1,500 to $2,500, going as high in some cases as $20,000. So it means that divorces before parliament are very expensive and the length of time taken to obtain them is long and can be very costly.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the current session of parliament we have discussed individually some divorce bills that came before us. The press, radio and other media
Procedure Committee
have given consideration to the matter of divorce as it has been discussed in this chamber and this has created much interest, not only with respect to the principle we raised of removing divorce from parliament but with respect to the wider field of divorce law. This has produced some interesting results. Not long ago on its program called "Close Up" the C.B.C. had a young lady appear-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member should confine his remarks about divorce to the question of parliament dealing with any procedure in divorce. We are not interested at this time in the substance involved in divorce. In my view it would be outside the scope of this discussion to deal with other than procedural problems.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not going into that field. One report on that broadcast had this to say:
Some of the fuss borders on burlesque. In Ottawa, for instance, Senator Roebuck, a lawyer, has been reported as suggesting that the woman and the C.B.C. should be prosecuted for disseminating false information and evidence. If Senator Roebuck spoke out instead for modernizing the crazy law which made the program possible he would have been doing this nation a greater service.
The report goes on to say-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. With all due respect I think the hon. member is getting away from procedural problems into the substance of the matter when he refers to the divorce law itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
What we have attempted to do in the house is remove divorce from the jurisdiction and responsibility of parliament but others have raised other considerations the interest in which I believe will continue to grow in the months and years ahead.
Much has been said about some things that happened here in this chamber. I have in my hand a translation from Le Petit Journal of Montreal of an article entitled "Unscrupulous Detectives Make a Racket Out of Divorce" by Alain Stanke in which the author described an interview with one of these detectives. They had been discussing the price of a divorce. A portion of the article reads as follows:
Then he became more precise: "If your wife also wants a divorce, then it's in the bag. If she doesn't want one, it is still possible to get one, but the chances are it will cost you a little more. Have you a lawyer?"
"No-I don't know one-I don't know what one is supposed to do-*" I reply innocently.
"So much the better. You are always better off to start by getting your evidence, then you can go and see any lawyer at all. Otherwise it will cost you more. Normally, it takes $1,000 for a lawyer and his costs. As for us you have nothing to worry about. Our discretion is assured; we will give the evidence in Ottawa-it will not be the first time-"

Procedure Committee
It continues in that vein. The article highlights the problem we are faced with in dealing with the evidence presented by lawyers in the stereotyped hotel or motel divorce case.
The Senate can probably be excused for making some mistakes because of the sheer volume of the cases they handle. I am sure they get tired of asking the same type of questions. This year we had one or two cases which highlighted the points we have dealt with in each case.
I will refer to only one, the Eccles case, which was referred back to the miscellaneous private bills committee. The committee heard the conflicting evidence of the petitioner and the respondent. In this case, somebody obviously committed perjury. Collusion was also charged in the case. In my opinion, and in the opinion of many newspapers, many of the faults we say are inherent in most divorce cases that go through parliament were illustrated by the Eccles case.
The case has been referred to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) for a decision. The hon. gentleman has done what the house has always done with respect to these cases. He took the position that he was not concerned with it and that it should be referred back to the Senate. On the basis of questions I have directed to the minister on this subject we can assume very little will come of it.
I have a photostatic copy of a document, the presentation of a process server of the city of Montreal, in which it is charged that the address at which the lady in the case was served originally was the Y.M.C.A. Subsequently it was changed to No. 1248 at a certain street. To the best of my knowledge and information no such person resides at that address. I am also sure she was not at the Y.M.C.A. although someone probably accepted and signed the document there in the first place. On July 29, as reported at page 7192 of Hansard, I addressed a question to the Minister of Justice about the alleged perjury in the Eccles divorce case. The minister replied as follows:
The hon. member's question anticipate something which has not yet commenced, that is, an investigation by the R.C.M.P. A day or two ago I received a letter from the chief of the committees branch transmitting to me the report of the committee, and I also received a day or two ago the transcript of the evidence.
In considering this matter I have felt that inasmuch as the matters concern themselves with two possible species of misconduct, first collusion and second perjury, and inasmuch as either or both of these, if they occurred, occurred also and primarily with respect to the proceedings before the Senate committee, it should be only appropriate that I should communicate with the chairman of the Senate committee to see whether that

hon. Senator or his committee felt that there was further action their committee decided to take in the matter.
I again put this question to the Minister of Justice on August 3, and it appears that finally the Senate decided to do nothing about it and referred the matter back to the Minister of Justice who is now looking at it with a view to turning it over to the attorney general in Ontario or some place else.
This is not good enough. If we honestly think we should be handling divorce cases in parliament we should set up the machinery which would make it possible not to make such a farce out of the whole proceedings. This committee and the Senate committee are possibly the most expensive kangaroo courts that there are in any place in the world and the injustice of a kangaroo court-

On a point of order, the hon. member has referred to the committees of the Senate and the House of Commons as taking part in a kangaroo court. I suggest that that is unparliamentary, and the hon. member should be asked to withdraw that statement and if he does not withdraw it he should be told to withdraw it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not quite know what a kangaroo court is. I think it is not complimentary. It is not in order to talk slightingly of committees of this house or of the other place, and I hope the hon. member will rectify what he said in that respect.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If there is objection to the remark I will be happy to withdraw it. I did not mean it to be offensive. Kangaroo courts are courts which used to be held in the army and their verdict did not necessarily meet with the approval of the judicial authority. But we will withdraw it.

What about trained seal
court?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, it could be a trained seal court, because it is certainly a rubber stamp. I hold in my hand a copy of the Toronto Star containing an article headed: "Charge M. P. Divorce Job Rubber Stamp Process". This amounts to what I said, though perhaps it is expressed somewhat differently.
This is what Mr. Rogers said. He said he was strongly suspicious that the Eccles case is not the only one involving collusion and perjury which has gone through the house this session. Moreover I would point out that only 25 or 30 cases have gone through the house this session. In most of the cases, Mr. Rogers said, there were genuine grounds for divorce, but he did not think that adultery- the only grounds on which parliament grants: divorce-was really involved. He says that.

the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) says that the house does nothing else but rubber stamp these divorce bills. He continues:
It is very difficult to detect collusion or perjury or anything like that. We get the sworn evidence and all we can do is read it through. If there are glaring discrepancies, we will spot them but otherwise we have no way of even suspecting that everything is anything but above board.
The hon. member for Lincoln, (Mr. Smith) a third member of the committee, said he has never been entirely satisfied that parliament should be dealing with divorce cases. If it continues to handle them, he said, the Senate should be provided with some sort of machinery which will enable its divorce committees to make sure that divorces are not obtained through collusion and perjury.
There was a television broadcast the other day, and I will apologize if this is not a correct transcript; I took it off a tape. Senator Roebuck had this to say:
A marriage breaks up-it is gone.
It is no longer in existence except technically. And they say, how can we dissolve it? There is only one way and that is for one or the other to commit adultery or at least appear to commit adultery. So witnesses will come and describe one or other of them in an embarrassing position and we sit there solemnly and carefully giving it the very best that we've got in judgment-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is getting back again to the grounds for divorce or the substantive law of divorce. We are dealing with divorce bills as a procedure of parliament and not with the grounds for divorce, or the law which permits divorce.

On a point of order, may I draw the attention of the house to standing order No. 34(2) which says:
Mr. Speaker or the chairman, after having called the attention of the house, or of the committee, to the conduct of a member who persists in irrelevance, or repetition, may direct him to discontinue his speech, and if then the member still continues to speak, Mr. Speaker shall name him, or, if in committee, the chairman shall report him to the house.
I would ask that the hon. member should try to be relevant in his remarks.
On a point of order, I would point out that if that rule were rigidly enforced the house would be three quarters empty most of the time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was pointing out that everybody is of the opinion that there are certain things wrong with the procedure here. Senator Roebuck went on to say:
It may be that one or other of the parties commits adultery for the very purpose of getting a divorce.
The hon. member for Halifax, the chairman of our committee, pointed out on the same program that about 150 of these cases are
Procedure Committee
hotel and motel cases of which at least 50 per cent are dishonest or rigged. This statement coming from the chairman of the committee and the other statements I have quoted clearly show that we should be doing something about the present situation. Now is the time for action to be taken. I should like to read a short excerpt from a letter sent to Mr. Claude Gauthier, the secretary to the Prime Minister, and I would suggest that if the Prime Minister knows about these things, this is rather shameful conduct, too. There was a letter sent to the Prime Minister, I presume-

I rise on a point of order. I think the hon. member has imputed shameful conduct to another member of this house and I suggest, again, that he withdraw, and if he does not do so, that he should be ordered to withdraw.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Halifax is perfectly right. I was considering whether the reference to shameful conduct referred to the writer or to the recipient of the letter, and the hon. member for Halifax who raised this point of order has obviously concluded that it referred to the Prime Minister. I thought it referred to the Prime Minister, and that remark should certainly not have been made in the context of a debate in this house, and the hon. member for Timis-kaming ought certainly to withdraw it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not know if the Prime Minister was aware of this correspondence or not-
Withdraw.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member did not intend to impute shameful conduct to the Prime Minister he ought to make it clear that his remark was not intended to apply to the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do that, Mr. Speaker.
An excerpt from this letter reads as follows:
Now I am in a state of suspended animation, married yet not married, why! Simply, according to your letter, because a Mr. Howard and a Mr. Peters whom I have never heard of in my life before have decided that it should be so! What mysterious power do these hon. gentlemen have.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Again I must ask the hon. member to come back to the point of debate. He is now reading from a document which reflects on the conduct of himself and another member of the house, and it is quite out of order. What we are debating is a report of the committee on procedure and in so far as the procedure on private bills of divorce is related to that report it can be discussed. If the hon. member can bring

Procedure Committee
himself back to that point, I hope he will do so. Otherwise, I think perhaps he should discontinue.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to refer to some alternatives to the present arrangement, alternatives which I believe to be an improvement on the present procedure. The first would be that Quebec and Newfoundland should set up divorce courts of their own and deal with these cases. If this is not in keeping with the wishes of Newfoundland and Quebec, then I think my second suggestion would be equally good, namely that we should set up a federal divorce court in the exchequer court in the same way as they set up a divorce court in Britain under the admiralty and probates court. The $100,000 which is now paid annually in respect of the present procedure would more than support one or two judges and the clerks necessary to run such a divorce court. This court would sit only in the province of Ontario, in Ottawa, and it would handle divorces not only from the two provinces I have mentioned, but from other provinces.
A third alternative, and one which I consider a poor one, is that the Senate, which does not handle these matters too well, should have power to handle-
On a point of order, the hon. member is making disparaging remarks about the other body of parliament, which I submit is unparliamentary.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, I can express an opinion that I do not think these divorces have been handled properly in the Senate, or as well as they should be. I do not think that is unparliamentary.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it would be drawing rather a fine line to rule out comment on the procedure of handling of divorces before committees, which reflects no more than on the conduct of proceedings, but does not reflect on any particular member.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
If it was given the full authority to handle divorces, and all that parliament would be asked to do would be to endorse them, it would be in keeping with the bill before us now in the name of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton). This would be a method that I think would not be as good as some others.
Fourth, we could establish in Canada a domicile which would allow people to have Canadian domicile and, if they did, then they could get a divorce in any province that handles divorces in Canada. This would

probably be a satisfactory method of dealing with them without solving the problem at all.
Fifth, there are other methods such as allowing people to get United States divorces and recognizing them in Canada; but it seems to me that the answer to this problem is going to be devised only when the House of Commons and the Senate set up a joint committee and decide that they are going to solve the problem of parliamentary divorces.
Certainly this procedural motion is a step in the right direction because we are going to find that under the rules no matter what we do with it we cannot solve this problem, and that we are going to have to look farther afield. I think one of the places we should look is in the direction of a joint committee of both houses. I am quite sure that that committee will come up with the conclusion that we are going to have to divest ourselves of the responsibility that we really have never given much consideration to in the first place.
I think that Canada is ready to take the step that Australia, New Zealand and Britain have taken and set up a divorce court which will handle these matters in such a manner that the ends of justice will be served and the rights of the people themselves will be respected.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege. The hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) who just sat down stated in his remarks that members from the province of Quebec are refusing to shoulder their responsibilities with regard to divorce bills.
I think that the phrase "refusing or not accepting their responsibilities" is a reflection on the integrity and honour of Quebec members.
I must say, indeed, that if Quebec members refrain from taking part in discussions on divorce bills, they have two major reasons for doing so.
The first one pertains to civil law; the second one to religion.
From the point of view of civil law, the Civil Code in the province of Quebec provides that marriage can be dissolved only by the death of either of the contracting parties. Thus, if we spoke in favour of divorce bills, we would obviously run counter to existing Quebec law.
From a religious point of view, most Quebec members are practising Catholics, whose religion is opposed to divorce.

Consequently, we are not shirking our responsibilities as members of parliament; on the contrary, our stand in the matter is the one expected of us by our constituents.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at any length in such an elaborate discussion on the procedure of the house. I do feel however, that I should say a few words as a member of the committee appointed to consider the procedure of the House of Commons.
On the whole, the previous speeches have been pleasant and quite informative. I just want to add a few personal impressions and suggestions.
Of course, the purpose of that committee was, if possible, to improve the procedure of the house. One does not need to follow the debates of this house very long before realizing that the rules are often transgressed. As evidence of this I need only refer to the speech of the hon. C.C.F. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters), a typical example of how those rules are abused.
His whole speech was made up of halftruths if not untruths. He cast aspersions on the personality of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and of several members of this house.
As a newcomer in this house, I have not had an opportunity to make a thorough study of each and every rule which governs the proceedings in this house. In my view, there is more to be learned from listening than from speaking.
I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that proceedings here are not always edifying. They even reveal glaring abuses. Of course it is a right of hon. members to raise points of order or matters of privilege.
Reference has been made in this debate to ways of speeding up procedure, including the use of a vote recording machine. That is a worth-while suggestion.
If the proposals put forward were acted upon, private members might enjoy a little more family life.
Unfortunately, proceedings drag on and on. This year, we have been sitting 144 days, and apparently we are going to be here for some time yet.

You are talking too much.
Procedure Committee
Another hon. Member: Order.

Mr. Speaker, there are things that have to be said. But it seems that some members in the opposition fail to understand that some measure of control must be exercised in parliamentary procedure.
A number of committees have been set up. I am of those who believe that a great deal of work can be done in committee-thus sparing the house some delays-by expediting legislation which, after all, must meet the wishes of the people of Canada.
Just now, I referred to abuses. During this session, opposition members managed to deal with unemployment for 13 days, endlessly repeating the same things. In fact, the first speech made by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) sounds very much like the last one he made on the same subject. Indeed, if we compare his first speech with his last, we note very little difference between the two.
Like the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), I hope that the special committee will be established as early as possible during the next session, so as to enable its members to consider procedure properly and to improve the standing orders to the fullest extent.
