Mr. Speaker, as one who is still an apprentice in so far as the rules are concerned and the purposes behind the rules, I am somewhat hesitant at entering this debate. However, as one who is interested in seeing that the house gets down to business perhaps more directly I should like to make a few suggestions with respect to the rules. When some of us first came into the house we thought the rules seemed a bit cumbersome, but as we began to study the purposes behind our rules our judgments became less severe. There are some things, however, that perhaps can be done and the report that is before us recommends certain steps which I believe will streamline our procedure to a greater degree.
There are one or two points I should like to bring to the attention of the house that may help us achieve our purpose. The first one is in respect of standing order 56 which sets out the days on which motions are necessary before the house can resolve itself into committee of supply, and further states that after six such motions all the estimates of the various departments should be before the committee. The opposition has an opportunity on any of these six motions to present grievances which they would like to have discussed. I would suggest, as the result of a recent experience, that after these six motions have been disposed of and the estimates are all

Procedure Committee
before the committee of supply the motion to go into committee of supply should not be debatable but should be in the same category as the motion for interim supply or the consideration of the supplementary estimates. This would enable more time to be spent on the discussion of the estimates.
I would suggest that when the rules were amended in 1955, the rules committee must have had that in mind when they specifically stated there should be six debatable motions for supply and yet they exempted the motions for interim supply. We have had a recent experience in this field when after the six motions were disposed of and a motion was moved to go into committee of supply, a want of confidence motion was moved which precipitated a debate. This debate could have taken place on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I noticed that on page 9 of the report of the committee the recommendation is to give public bills precedence over private bills from five to six o'clock on Fridays. I believe this recommendation results from the fact that private bills have occupied so much of the time of the house this year that the discussion of certain public bills has been prevented. I did think that perhaps if this house were to continue to entertain divorce petitions we should set up a separate category for these petitions. However, I know that is something that will have to be given a great deal of study before we would commit ourselves to such a suggestion.
I was very interested in the references to the procedures in other parliaments such as the ones in India and in England, where a committee is set up composed of representatives of the various parties and time is allotted to the parties to discuss certain matters. As I understand it, these arrangements are not really binding on the house, but it is an effort to streamline the debate and perhaps get more directly to the points at issue. This might be a procedure that could be studied by this house. Some members have made suggestions that our committees are too large and they might be more efficient if they were composed of a smaller number of members. I agree with this suggestion.
I should like now to turn to a matter that has been troubling many hon. members in this house, namely the manner in which divorce bills are handled in this house. If I may be permitted I should like to refer to the fact that they were faced with the same problem in England before 1857. Over a period of 150 years prior to 1857 the parliament of England dealt with 230 divorces. They felt, because they had dealt with this number over this long period of time, that it was a cumbersome burden on their house and they

decided to do something about it. As a result, in 1857 the matrimonial causes act was passed by means of which divorce courts were established in that country. Here, in Canada, we have not had 230 cases over a period of 150 years, but this year we have had over 600 applications for divorce come before the two houses, the Senate and the House of Commons. Reference has been made to the fact that about 500 of these bills are still to be passed. There has been an average of 300 divorce bills each year for the last 10 years.
The problem was much easier of solution in England because there is just the one jurisdiction. It was only a matter of convincing the people who were opposed to divorce that if there were to be divorces granted there was a more efficient way of handling them. Unfortunately, in Canada, it is not as easy. I should like to try to bring this question into some perspective so that we may better understand it because a great deal of confusion has arisen as a result of accusations made in the press concerning the manner in which evidence is obtained for divorce proceedings. Even in our courts in Ontario there has been a cloud as to how evidence in divorces has been obtained, even under a judicial system. I think that with these accusations being made we should not cloud the issue until we see the problem that we have in proper perspective. What is the reason that these cases are before us in any event?
The previous speaker from the C.C.F. party mentioned that here is a matter where certain citizens in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland have a right, shall I say, to obtain something that they cannot obtain in any other forum. Since this house has jurisdiction to deal with divorce, they as private individuals petition the parliament of Canada in order that they may obtain some right of action to overcome their matrimonial difficulties.
I think we would be rather hasty to deny these people their right to apply here for a divorce. We would be denying them a fundamental right, just because it is a divorce, when for some other reason they may want to come to parliament to have their rights protected. But the fact that we do not want to deny them their rights does not necessarily say that this is the proper forum for divorce.
But having that in mind, Mr. Speaker, let us look at the proper role of the committee in dealing with these divorces. I think the committee of the House of Commons, the same as the committee in the Senate, must try to take the same perspective, the same

Procedure Committee
outlook as if they were judges in a court dealing with a divorce action that is brought before them.
There is some dispute whether that committee is acting as a court or is acting as an arm of the legislative body. Many of us feel that parliament as such is the supreme court of the country, and as such the committee of that parliament should carry out judicial functions. It is true that the committee has much more than judicial functions; it also has legislative functions. It also has the power, if it so wishes, to grant a divorce on any ground whatsoever.
And does.

The hon. member says, "And does". I would dispute that. However, with that perspective in mind, a petition comes before the committee of the other place. That committee, using rules that they have set up and the best judgment that they have, come to certain decisions. Their decisions are then forwarded to this house in the form of a private bill. That private bill is in due course referred to a committee of our house and it is dealt with there by the members of the committee in a judicial capacity. Unless there is something very drastically wrong on the surface with the bill that is brought before it, the committee usually passes the bill in rather short order and, as some of us have said, we have more or less rubber-stamped the bill.
But there are a number of bills which we, in our examination, are suspicious of and cause further investigation to be made, and perhaps call witnesses or send them back to the other place for further consideration. Then a number of bills come before us that are disputed, where in effect we are made a court of appeal of the decision made in the other place. At that time the committee must sit as a court of appeal.
I think if we were to give the committee the proper designation and were not to falsely criticize its role we would realize that a person making an appeal before that committee must prove the facts that he alleges on the appeal the same as he would in any other court of appeal in the province. He has the right, I believe-although it has been stated that we have been advised to the contrary-to ask to bring witnesses before us, and I understand there are forms prepared which can ask for witnesses to be subpoenaed.
It has been stated that we have not the power to pay for these witnesses. But, Mr. Speaker, that is not the function, nor is it necessary, because it will be recalled that in any of our courts across the country everyone has a right to subpoena a witness
before the court, but the party who subpoenas that witness-who wants the witness-must pay for him to appear before the court. Therefore, when any of these cases come before the committee it is up to the party concerned to pay for the witnesses. They are making an appeal before the committee and it is up to them to have these witnesses there to prove the things which they allege. It is not our fault if they do not appear before the committee to substantiate the things which they allege.
The committee can do no more than any other court in the land but to dismiss an appeal, to dismiss an allegation that is not proved. It is not our function to go out and investigate and take sides. If there is any situation such as arose in the Eccles case, as we did in that case, we would refer it to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the Minister of Justice would refer it to the proper authorities.
I would make this suggestion with respect to certain charges of perjury and collusion. The better way of handling such suspicions as these would be to send them back to the other place where these allegations had been committed against that forum, and let them deal with them or get the proper authorities to deal with them. The suggestion was made that because we have before us conflicting evidence-yes, even diametrically opposed evidence-and we must choose between it, that someone must be committing perjury and we must therefore go out and hunt to find out who was right and who was wrong, and perhaps bring charges of perjury.
I would suggest that every day in our courts there are cases that come before them where evidence is diametrically opposed, or differs, and in very rare cases do the judges go out of their way to suggest that the losing party should be investigated for perjury. I think perhaps it might go too far to say that everyone who has lost has committed perjury. I think we should be very careful in our accusations along that line.
With that in mind and believing that that is the true function of our committee and its operations, when we are considering the rules today and are considering the problems we should consider them in that light. I and many others feel that this committee is not adequate to deal with these problems that come before us, because I believe that the committee on divorce that we have is too large in the first place to deal with these things when it comes to an appeal or trial. It is all right if we are going through the evidence and agreeing with the evidence that has gone through the other place. When it comes to a point that we have to hear the

Procedure Committee
evidence de novo I do not feel that we have adequate powers to deal with it.
There can be another injustice, that toward the end of a session the committee can be put in a very severe dilemma. Someone brings an appeal, and it becomes difficult to get the witnesses before the committee before the house prorogues. As we all know, when parliament prorogues this session all bills which have not been passes through all stages are then lost. Here we have a dilemma, that we see either by affidavit or by a statement an application for an appeal, and if we accept it and call for a hearing but in the meantime the house prorogues, then in effect we have dismissed that action without having heard the pros or cons of the case. If we are required for a few years or so to continue wrestling with this problem, I would suggest power be granted to hold over such cases so they would not lose the preliminary steps taken to date toward making them law, and at the next session of parliament we could continue to deal with the next stage of the matter.
A number of suggestions have been made as to what we should do to remedy this situation. Annoyed as many of us may be at having to deal with these matters, I think we must look at the thing squarely, recognizing the rights and the beliefs of those concerned and see what compromise can be made. There are three methods, as has been stated before, whereby this matter might be dealt with.
First of all, the matter could be referred back to the provinces concerned and dealt with as in other provinces. This would be the most efficient way of dealing with it because the provinces have the power to deal with the disposition and custody of the children of the marriage, as well as matters of alimony and maintenance as between the aggrieved parties. In that way the whole matter could be dealt with in a sort of package deal.
I am coming to the belief that it is not just a matter of providing a divorce court. All these cases for divorce should be processed through what we call a family court first and every attempt made by counsellors of marriage and those who have made a study of what causes the break-up of homes in order to see if these people could not be brought together again. A great deal has been done, but it is not for me to pursue that matter at this time.
The other method would be to set up a division of the exchequer court or even to set up some other court altogether to deal with all these cases judicially, and I think we could do this constitutionally. But the great weakness in that is that the court could

only dissolve the marriage. It could not deal with the rights of the children, nor could it deal with maintenance or alimony, because they are matters which pertain to the provinces. But it would clear the House of Commons and the other place of this problem of dealing with divorces, and as a judicial body I feel they could deal with that aspect of it more efficiently than we could. As a second best method I would suggest we work toward that end.
However, perhaps being a realist I think we may not be ready politically for that move, although I can see no difference if we are going to deal with divorces in this house between dissolving a marriage here or dissolving it in an exchequer court or any other court we may set up. There is no different sanction if it were dealt with judicially than if it were dealt with in a semi-judicial manner by parliament.
As I have said, I have a bill on the order paper, Bill No. C-17, in which I suggest we give power to the other house to deal with divorces exclusively. But I would like to make this one additional suggestion which is not included in the bill. In order to overcome certain constitutional difficulties and the objections of those who would not like to see the business of the House of Commons transferred to the other place, I suggest that this house pass an act annually to the effect that every bill passed by the other place authorizing the dissolution of marriage once it has received royal assent shall be considered law.
There is a precedent for this type of procedure in the parliament of the United Kingdom where under an act of 1911, as a result of a dispute between the House of Lords and the House of Commons, the House of Commons, having had a bill passed three times by that house but rejected three times by the House of Lords, may now pass the bill which on receiving royal assent will become law without having been passed by the House of Lords.
Perhaps that is a precedent which we would not like to extend here, but it might be a temporary method of dealing with the problem we have, and by passing an annual act we are not completely depriving this house of its jurisdiction in that field. If that were done I suggest the other place would provide in addition to their committee which deals with bills as they go through a committee which would act as a sort of court of appeal for all those bills under dispute so that any matter could be given a second look and the party concerned would have an appeal to them as they have an appeal presently to this house.

I know that this is a matter which perhaps cannot be dealt with logically because of certain strong feelings of many members concerned. I feel that the members of the C.C.F. party in perhaps a sincere effort to bring this matter before the public have placed themselves and this house in a rather severe dilemma. Because if by a method of what some of us call a filibuster-what they have called careful consideration of those bills-[DOT] we have delayed or prevented their passage we are preventing the rights of these people from being properly attended to in the only form available to them at the present time. That is not doing any good in the sense of persuading those who should give them the right to do so, because in those provinces the forces behind the government there say, "We do not want to permit divorce in this province. You are only helping us to prevent those people getting their divorce. We say they should not have a divorce and we thank you for not letting them get a divorce by not letting them go to the House of Commons". I know that is not their purpose but that is in effect what would happen if we follow through logically the tactics being used.
In effect they are trying to force the government to adopt a procedure to remedy the situation which, to be dealt with logically, effectively and correctly would be trying to force the provinces to do something which it is within their rights to refuse. I do not think any government is going to be placed in that position and politically, I am sure, members on this side are not going to alienate themselves by forcing those provinces to do something which they do not want to do. That might cause our defeat, but it certainly would not bring the C.C.F. to power. It might bring the Liberals back to power and perhaps the hon. member for Timiskaming and his friends would prefer them to us-

Anything would be better
than the Tories.

However, I do not think that is the purpose which they have in mind. I do not know. I suggest we must consider not only the logic of the situation but the rights and feelings of others. We must not force those who are not ready for this move into a position which would make them even more antagonistic to a change. A great deal of education still remains to be done. I think we should also bear in mind that although we are dealing here primarily with procedures inside this house, a much greater debate with respect to divorce is raging not only in the provinces where these bills originate but in other provinces. A great deal of study must be given to this question
Procedure Committee
before we can be assured that we are setting out a proper procedure. I should like to suggest that perhaps the time has come when the authorities of government at both dominion and provincial levels, the religious leaders of the country and the social workers of the country should get together at a conference and study this whole matter of divorce and divorce procedures in its wider aspect and consider how it may be dealt with, because divorce is a cancerous growth in the family institution which is weakening that institution. It is one of the great evils of our society and the sooner we wake up to this menace and the sooner we attack the problem on a scientific social basis the better it will be for our country.
This question of the procedure in the House of Commons is only one small part of a much wider and deeper subject. I hope the people of this country will wake up and not ignore the problem any longer. It is not a matter of making divorce easier, but a matter of preventive training and making sure that those who marry are given proper training and that if there are any difficulties proper study is given to their problems.

Perhaps I should say a word or two. Perhaps, like the hon. member for Davenport, I should make a comment or two first about the rules of the house in connection with the changes which have been made by the committee, other than dealing with divorces.
Without going into the detailed changes about hours, time allotted for debate and things of that nature, there is one matter which I think should occupy the concern and interest of parliament and of hon. members in the opposition particularly. This is a matter which I have thought about and considered for some time, and my thoughts apply to whatever government is in power. It merely happens to be a Conservative government at the moment. These are things which I think perhaps cannot be dealt with by alterations in the rules themselves.
There seems to have been over the years a growing increase in the authority of the government in office over parliament through the party system, and a decline in the functions as it were of the individual private member. The desire which we all have for independence of expression and for casting our votes on particular issues in parliament based upon what we think, has in recent years been stifled to a degree by the party control that exists within the Conservative party, as it exists within other parties. I submit, however, that, generally speaking, control of this sort on a party basis is stronger on the government side than it is

Procedure Committee
on the opposition side, and this is true of any government when it is in office. I think this is true of the government in Saskatchewan which is of the same party as I am, which does not make it any more tolerable or acceptable.
I do not think this party control is compatible with our sense of democracy or with our sense of promoting the interests of our constituencies as best we can. Too often we find that motions critical of the government are looked upon as falling within the class of being want of confidence motions. Opposition amendments or proposals are accepted in some cases, but in many cases they are rejected out of hand as it were, and again the house is divided on a party basis. I do not believe that this leads to holding the balance of our democratic system in parliament, and I should like to see it reduced as much as possible and, as far as possible, a return to the right of individual members to independence of thought, independence of speech and independence when it comes to voting. I think there may be some differences of opinion as to the means by which this objective may best be achieved. My own views are merely injected into the debate at this stage as an indication of how this problem may be approached.
It may be that the debate on the budget, the debate on the address and the debates which take place on the various supply motions afford ample opportunity for the opposition parties in parliament to express lack of confidence in the government on a variety of subjects. Possibly legislation which is closely connected with the budget proposals, such as taxation and things of that nature, should also fall within a stricter category. Government sponsored bills should not be looked upon as ones in which the party should control their ultimate destiny.
When individual private members regardless of party introduce bills, as some have done this session although we have been restricted in debating them, they should automatically go to a committee for study and consultation with government officials from the department and with the minister concerned to clarify the bill or bring it into line with existing legislation. These bills often represent the views of an hon. member concerning alterations in legislation. They should not be allowed to die on the order paper whether or not they are debated. We should attempt to put these things into effect so the independence of private members will be enhanced more than in the past. Then we would have the kind of government we had when responsible government came into being. Government should be responsible to parliament and not the other way round.

My primary concern is to deal with divorce procedure and alternate methods as was dealt with by the hon. members for Vancouver East, Timiskaming and Davenport. As the hon. member for Davenport put it, there may be some concern on the part of individual members who are angry at the hon. member for Timiskaming and myself for carrying on such a detailed study of these bills. Perhaps some of their concern stems from the fact that they had introduced private bills which they would have liked to see debated. That is understandable. I am angry at myself because I caused six of my own bills to die on the order paper because of my extended debate on divorce. Other hon. members have beeen angry at us for other reasons. We have been concerned about the unfortunate feeling that existed and perhaps still exists. We felt this matter was so important that we could not alter our course regardless of the pressure exerted on us or the individual expressions of anger directed to us from inside the house and outside of it. We have caused grief and anxiety in the minds and hearts of those who have in good faith petitioned for divorce. We have great concern, interest and sorrow-
For yourself.
-for any anxiety we have caused them.
Can you restore the sanity of a woman who lost it because of your actions? Can you do that?
Mr. Speaker, I am on my feet so I do not have to rise on a point of order.
I will ask that question on my feet.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Halifax rising on a point of order?
No, Mr. Speaker, I had a question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Skeena rising to deal with the subject matter before the house?

Yes. My point of order has to do with the interjection made by the hon. member for Halifax. He has a great propensity for making interjections while in his seat and I submit this should be brought to his attention.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is quite right in bringing to the attention of the Chair that interjections should not be made by an hon. member from his seat.
If the hon. member for Halifax wishes to put his question I will be glad to answer it. Apparently he does not.

Mr. Speaker, I simply
wanted to ask the hon. member for Skeena whose cup is overflowing with sorrow this evening whether or not he could bring back sanity to a woman who has lost it because of his actions.

I did not know I was considered in the class of a psychiatrist. I do not know what 1 can do in so far as this woman is concerned. If I tried to restore the sanity of the hon. member for Halifax I know I would fail.
The report of this committee contains some interesting factors. On the committee along with yourself, Mr. Speaker-incidentally, you did a commendable job-were three important cabinet ministers, even if I would like to do away with the salary of one of them. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) was one. He has under study now one of the divorce proceedings. Another was the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), a distinguished hon. member and leader of the house. The other was the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer). They participated in this study and endorsed the recommendations concerning divorce procedure. This indicates that they did not act independently and I am sure this reflects cabinet approval. They had approval to deal with these questions in this way at this time. There is some doubt as to whether the problem of private bills of divorce is capable of procedural solution, as is stated in the report.
The report recommends that a similar committee be appointed early in the next session to continue the studies made including a study of the procedure on divorce bills. I hope the members of the committee next year conclude that this problem is not capable of a procedural solution and perhaps the alternatives outlined by the hon. member for Timiskaming could be considered. Possibly a joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate could be set up to deal with these other alternatives. This could be completed before the end of the next session, whether it is next fall as intimated or in January of next year.
The procedural committee could be established almost immediately next session to study the question. If it concludes that the problem does not lend itself to a procedural solution it could report back recommending the establishment of a royal commission or joint committee or some other method of studying the alternatives, and solutions could be found before the end of next session. If that course is followed we will perhaps find, if not a complete solution at least a partial one leading to a final one, even if it is the solution advocated by the hon. member for
Procedure Committee
Davenport which I understand will be put forward by other hon. members.
The hon. member for Timiskaming and I, principally, and a couple of other hon. members have made a detailed study and examination of these divorce bills. The petitioners who petitioned parliament during this session did so in good faith. Of course, the way in which divorce bills were handled in years past would indicate that there would be no difficulty in having divorces granted or their divorce bills passed provided the evidence adduced before the committee met the rules laid down by that committee, and on that basis the petitioners had every reason to expect that their divorces would be granted.
However, they suddenly came to realize that this was not the position this session because without warning-I admit this without hesitation-the hon. member for Timiskaming	(Mr. Peters)	and	I	proceeded toexamine	and study the	bills	in	detail. It maybe said	that this was	sort	of	unfair to thepetitioners, and that is quite true. This is one of the main and major compelling reasons, coupled with the fact that our campaign has met with a great degree of success, as witness the debate we are having at the present time, why we feel it would be most unwise and unfair this session to proceed further	with any detailed	examination of
these particular bills.
Perhaps if this motion passes in a short time and the next order having to do with private bills is called there will be no difficulty in getting wholesale automatic passage of the various bills on the order paper. However, I think the activity this year would indicate very clearly and definitely that the possibilities of this thing occurring in future years are great. I refer to the possibility of detailed examination of divorce bills in the years to come so long as they remain a part of the business of parliament. I think that each lawyer in the province of Quebec and Newfoundland who is approached in the months to come to take action or to represent a petitioner for a bill of divorce should in good faith indicate to that petitioner that the chances of a bill of divorce passing in parliament in future sessions are very slim indeed, because of the detailed examination that has taken place this year, and so long as they remain a part of the business of this house and debate on them is allowed perhaps the same course will be followed in the future, and I submit that this is what will happen and that people should be informed accordingly.
As I said, this year the petitioners petitioned in good faith, fully expecting no

Procedure Committee
difficulty. For the difficulties they have encountered we are extremely sorry but no further difficulties will be encountered by them this session.
I listened to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) with extreme interest. I think he made an excellent presentation and supported the idea we are propounding. If I wanted to have counsel to plead argument for me in this particular matter I could do no better in this entire House of Commons than to retain the hon. member for Davenport to plead the particular case and set forth those particular arguments. I would, of course, give him a little guidance on the way he should tackle the matter but in general his presentation was excellent.

We think a lot of
ourselves, don't we?

I am saying that in a gentle way only to show that I disagree with some of the points the hon. member for Davenport made, but in spite of that disagreement, which is slight, I say he made an excellent contribution and argument in favour of a certain course of action with which I generally agree. I would have given him a little bit of guidance; if he happened to be counsel for me I would ask him to argue in a certain way.
If hon. members take the course of action on this question of divorce proceedings in the house this evening that is suggested it will solve the matter at least temporarily for next year without any difficulty. I submit the motion before us at the moment could be proceeded with rather quickly. I imagine the debate had almost concluded when I rose and it could be completed rather quickly. The government could forgo calling any further government orders and we would then proceed with the next item on the order paper which is private bills relating to divorce. They could be dispatched, I am sure, in a moment, and the next item on the order paper to be dealt with is public bills and orders and we could then proceed with the bill in the name of the hon. member for Davenport. We could then debate it and pass it and after it was passed by the Senate it would become law. If this action were taken it would be applauded by every member in the house. I am sure there would be no objection to it. I do not know whether this course of action is acceptable to the government but I submit it for consideration at this time as perhaps a tentative step in the direction of modernizing our divorce laws in Canada.
The hon. member for Davenport also dealt with procedure and I hope I will be permitted to follow his line of reasoning. Many others

have mentioned what takes place before the committee in the other place, the manner in which these bills get there and what happens to them when they get here. We have had occasion as you know, sir, to look at, examine and discuss in some detail the evidence taken before the committee of the other place. The procedure of parliament in dealing with divorces I submit allows us to examine the evidence.
Some of the bills which we have already examined in the past shows that there is an extreme amount of concern on the part of those asking questions and hearing the evidence with respect to the question of desertion. Questions are asked as to whether there has been desertion and a relatively minor amount of concern is taken in the evidence respecting adultery. The prepon-derence of questioning is on desertion. In some instances the evidence of adultery is flimsy. Certainly that is what we found in some of the bills we examined. I am sure that members of the other place and members of our committee vote in favour of granting a particular divorce not on the grounds of adultery, although there is evidence to that effect, but primarily on the evidence given with respect to desertion. I submit that in a roundabout way that is what we are doing.
The same thing applies if there is extensive examination of witnesses with respect to cruel action on the part of the respondent, whether there were beatings, whether there was alcoholism, whether there were other activities of a similar nature which could be classified as cruelty, and relatively little examination of the flimsy evidence in so far as adultery is concerned. I submit that in so far as the evidence is concerned or in so far as the rules of the other place are concerned, divorces in fact have been passed by the members of the other place and by some of the members here on the grounds and on the basis of evidence with respect to cruelty.
I submit that these are subject matters which should be considered, and the substantive law changed in so far as divorce is concerned to include these subject matters as grounds for divorce.
This, of course, is getting into the substance of the question itself, and I do not want to transgress on your rulings, Mr. Speaker. I only raise this in a slight way in order to indicate that at the next session, if the committee on procedure is re-established and it should find, as I am sure it will, that it is not possible, not advantageous, not desirable to proceed in the manner we have or in any other similar manner by which divorces may be handled in parliament or to

find an alternative step, then something should be done by means of a joint committee or a royal commission or whatever mode the government chooses in order to examine in detail not only the mechanics by which divorces are granted, either in parliament or through some other agency, but also the grounds upon which divorces are granted. This would be a means of bringing our divorce laws into a position where they would be more compatible with those in other countries so that we will have some sense instead of hyprocrisy applying to divorce procedures in Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I asked the hon. member not to pursue that line because, as he knows and has already suggested himself, it goes beyond the scope of the debate.

Mr. Speaker, in a few moments I will give some sort of consideration to the thoughtful contribution made by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) on the vexatious question of parliamentary divorce, and also answer the sundry remarks that have been made by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). Before I turn to the motion which arises out of the work of the committee, there are two points which should be made about the contribution of the hon. member for Skeena who spoke soulfully about the rights of private members which have been practically denied, at least in the private members' hours this session, because of the divorce filibuster. I would suggest that one knows a person by his actions rather than by his words. It would be a bitter day for private members in any parliament in which the hon. member for Skeena had any position of authority.

I rise on a point of order. I object strenuously to these slanderous accusations against my actions in the house. The hon. member has suggested that if I had authority I would remove the rights of private members. I suggest that he should be asked not only to withdraw but also to refrain from making these scandalous accusations in the future.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member will withdraw the word "slanderous", I will deal with the other matter.
Yes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point the hon. member makes is that in what the hon. member for Halifax said he had imputed some improper conduct which could be expected from the hon. member if he were to occupy a position of authority. If that was the purport of the
Procedure Committee
remarks of the hon. member for Halifax, and I am not clear that it was, I am sure he would wish to modify such a statement.

Of course, I will modify those remarks.
The second point I want to make about the contributions of the hon. member for Skeena concerns his suggestion that the lawyers in Quebec and Newfoundland tell the people in those two provinces that they could not always be guaranteed the right to a divorce in parliament in the future. The answer to that point is very easy, Mr. Speaker. The main burden of parliament is now in the hands of people of the calibre of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and we are not going to be held up by the actions of one or two members, no matter what their feelings on this particular subject may be. I think that that message can be passed along to the lawyers in Quebec and Newfoundland, too.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And let us see who wins.
Oh, oh.

That is typical of the contributions these hon. members make from their seats. They do not like it if somebody else uses that tactic against them. If I have fallen into bad habits, and perhaps I have, it is because I learned them from these two hon. members.
Timber, timber.

I will be back to you in a moment, and in great detail; that is not a threat, it is an actuality.
The purpose of the committee report, and I had the honour of serving with you, Mr. Speaker, and the other distinguished members of the House of Commons on the committee, is to provide a more flexible and practical method of handling the affairs of parliament. We wish to provide a means by which an earlier start can be made on government business without in any way hurting the rights of private members in the way they have been hurt this session. As I see the session of the House of Commons, it divides itself into three main parts. The first part is the throne speech debate, the first votes of confidence in the government, and then a number of private members' days, very proper days and very important ones from my point of view. The second part we might almost give exclusively to the minister of finance, who deals with the budget, then the budget resolutions and any legislation arising out of them. The third part would be concerned with the bulk of the government's program.

Procedure Committee
It was the purpose of your committee, sir, and I gather all members support the suggestion, that we do make an earlier start on government business and get the committees of the house functioning earlier. I think back to my earlier years, all of which have been extremely pleasant except this one, and I find that in the first part of the session most of the members seem to become bored or restless. Then during the second half of the session they are worked to death. Of course, parliamentary reform must lie within the hearts and minds of the members. If we were to put ourselves under discipline in the dramatic fashion of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee), who limits himself to 15-minute speeches, then we would get through our work sooner and not bore each other in the process.
Then another point which I think perhaps could be solved by the rules committee in future years, not this year, is to provide more variety in private members' days, the eight of them in a session, so that we could deal with more resolutions and more bills. Frequently a debate will start on a very interesting piece of legislation, the mover of which has a direct interest in it and he will bring a great deal of variety into that debate. However, by the middle of the afternoon or an hour or two later, it simply becomes a matter of talking things out in a rather pedestrian fashion. Perhaps the committee could give some consideration to this matter, so that the points of view on different matters that are pets to private members can be deliberated.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this is one of those rare occasions upon which no one has claimed the paternity of the ideas concerning the reference in the committee report to procedural reforms for divorce in parliament. I will let you in on a secret, sir, which you already know, but of which perhaps all hon. members are not aware, that it was something I raised and asked the committee if it would be good enough to hear my views on the matter of procedural reform for divorce.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

Those who know me here, and I think have some faith in me, know that I would not willingly see any abuse of any existing procedure if I thought there were methods of clearing it up. I think the hon. member had a question.

I wonder if my friend from Halifax could indicate if he presented these views that he is putting forward to the committee itself when the committee was meeting?
[Mr. McCleave.1
I asked that; but I have drawn up a very rough draft of the points I would like raised in the committee, which will be circulated as soon as I have completed that memorandum. Is that the question?
No. I understood the hon. member for Halifax to say that in so far as the committee investigating the question of divorce is concerned, he himself raised that with the committee.
That is right, Mr. Speaker, I did.
Another question. When the committee was being established in the house, did the hon. member hear us suggest that this would be a proper course of action for the committee to take?

Then perhaps I did not listen to the hon. member at that time. If he did make that suggestion, it undoubtedly was a wise one. But nobody else brought it up in the rules committee, so I did myself. I hope that answers the question.
So it is my desire, as a person charged with a difficult responsibility and a rather thankless one, to do the best I can with it and to play my part with others by being the conscience of the House of Commons as a whole to see that things are proceeded with as properly as possible.
The hon. members of the C.C.F. are apparently willing to allow the remainder of the divorce bills to go through on the understanding that the procedural problems of divorce will be studied, and this is a very fine gesture. I wish to refer the house to the Journals of the House of Commons for Saturday, July 18, 1959. That is a little over a year ago, Mr. Speaker. At that time I presented a report from the committee which says in part:
Your committee has considered three hundred and fifty three (353) divorce bills sent from the Senate and rejected one during the current session.
Your committee found itself seriously handicapped because there are no standing orders applicable to the procedure in committee such as exists in the other place.
Your committee strongly recommends that when it is reconstituted next session it be empowered, with the help of the chief of the committees and private legislation branch and the law officers of the house, to draft rules of procedure for its guidance and to submit these to the house for consideration by the standing committee on standing orders.
That was put by you, Mr. Speaker, at that time and accepted. The point is that we are now getting, or I hope we will get by the vote of the house later this evening or tomorrow, what was asked for by the committee over a year ago. But a lot of time has been

wasted on the so-called detailed examination d! the divorce problem in the meantime.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? In what relationship would the matter of the detailed examination delay the passing of the recommendation of the committee of three years ago?

I think the hon. member has been around long enough to know the mood of the House of Commons as well as I do. Mr. Speaker, may I turn to some of the practical matters that need reform on a procedural level. The hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) mentioned this afternoon the problem of summoning witnesses, and he confused two situations that can arise in dealing with this problem. The house and the committee does have the power to issue a summons for either party to require witnesses to come to the committee. What it apparently does not have is the right for the committee itself to issue such summonses to ask people to appear before it. These are substantially different things. I was very sorry to hear the attack made on the law clerk of the House of Commons late this afternoon by the hon. member for Timiska-ming, when he made a reference to the committee not having competent legal advice. Dr. Maurice Ollivier has been around here for 35 years. He has advised prime ministers and others during that time on some of the most important constitutional and other legal problems that can arise in Canada. I am sorry that I was not quicker on my feet to suggest to the hon. member that he would not like to leave such a remark on the record against a very devoted, dedicated, first-rate servant of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear.

As for his remarks about myself, I do not think I have to answer them. I could put it this way, that if any member of the Conservative party, or any member of the Liberal party-just one member, Mr. Speaker-were to object to my fairness. my integrity or my honesty in these matters, then I would withdraw from the committee.
Hear, hear.

Another matter that demands procedural reform, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton), or at least he pointed out the problem that can arise, is the time to contest cases. There are two types of cases. One is where all matters have been thoroughly at issue before the other place and then come before us, which is properly a matter for us of course to consider. Sometimes jocularly 79951-0-491
Procedure Committee
we call ourselves the chamber of sober second thought on these divorce matters. On other matters, and we have had three of them this session, people have come to parliament very late to say they were not served properly, there was collusion, or there were other matters that were not brought out before the committee of the other place. Here we need a procedural reform, it seems to me, to see that such cases shall go back to the other place so that they may deal with them, if that was the judicial process that was abused in the first place.
The matter of the service of relevant documents in the case has not been raised, I think. None the less, it is very important. There have been abuses this year, particularly by a Montreal detective named Charles Char-ron. The chairman of the other place, with whom I work quite closely, has made it a point to circularize the Montreal bar that in no instances are proceedings in divorce cases to be served by a detective who was involved in the investigation of the case. That is a very useful reform that is needed.
Then we should consider renumbering the cases so they are more intelligible to members of the House of Commons. Perhaps we should also figure out some way where a judicial procedure will not be abused by what is called the process of talking out. The hon. member for Timiskaming mentioned with some pride that he had been instrumental in talking a case out of parliament. That case was a very hard fought one. There were bitter passions on both the pros and cons of the case, and certainly there was a great division of our own. Perhaps in cases where the decision of the committee is so close it is legitimate to talk it out and leave the parties to come back next year. Otherwise I think it is simply an abuse to use parliamentary devices to deny justice to people who do petition us.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), in an otherwise good speech, praised the accomplishments of the hon. members for Skeena and Timiskaming and what they had done this year. In the first place, I have shown that they have done precisely nothing, because the motion we are going to approve later tonight is simply, in its divorce section, something that has existed before parliament as a recommendation for 13 months.
I would also point out that in my remarks on the bill of rights I mentioned some of the great social mischief that had been caused by the filibuster, and it is mischief that can never really properly be repaired. I hope that when the history and the pros and cons of this are written up the journalists will make

Procedure Committee
some study of just what effect this has had on the little man and woman of Quebec and Newfoundland.
One of the things that cheered me on this whole matter was right around the House of Commons in our corridors among our own servants who said, "Keep after these fellows and do not let them push these people around". That has been my object and intention all along, and it will be my object and intention if I am ever again mixed up in one of these divorce filibusters.
One of the hon. members said that this was not a judicial proceeding, and he quoted a law book that is slightly out of date. I would simply refer him to the Criminal Code, section 99 (c), which defines what a judicial proceeding is. That section reads:
(c) "judicial proceeding" means a proceeding ...
(ii) before the Senate or House of Commons of Canada or a committee of the Senate or House of Commons... that is authorized by law to administer an oath,-
I think that should solve that matter. It was put very ably the other day by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) in the presence of the two hon. members but they were not listening.
Now some further thoughts on judicial proceedings. A judicial proceeding to me involving members of this house is a proceeding in which the members do not take sides before the particular case comes on for trial. They do not investigate it, but when it is properly contested they leave it up to the lawyer or to the witnesses for both parties. I would like to think that that was the example followed by all hon. members but I know from looking over the voting record of two members in regard to all the cases which have come forward this year and in previous years, whenever one party has made contact with those members they have invariably voted for that party.
Would you like to name the two members?

Yes; I would like to name the two members and refer to the cases. The two members are the hon. member for Timiskaming and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), and the cases are Eccles, Freeman and Walker.
Would the hon. member permit a question. Does he know that I have consistently voted against every divorce case coming before parliament?

I was told that while I was away the hon. member for Skeena was good enough to second a divorce case on my behalf.

One of the hon. members also mentioned what he called the failure of Quebec members to attend the miscellaneous private bills committee. I know one member who has attended almost twice as many meetings as the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Timiskaming combined.
Yet another abuse of judicial procedure. One hon. member made a statement. He had a chance to cross-examine on it earlier, but he made a statement to the committee which, if accepted, could have meant that a case would have been thrown out instead of the petition being granted. Fortunately there was another member there who could correct that misstatement of fact.
Those are very serious matters. If the hon. members say that this is not a judicial procedure, I think it is right if they do not bring the qualities of heart and mind to that body properly to judge cases. But I would not allow that to be said of members of the Conservative or members of the Liberal parties who have gone there with open minds and waited until all the evidence was in before deciding the cases.
Finally, on this point, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Davenport asked whether public opinion can be changed to deal with these divorce cases. I think that is up to the people of Quebec and Newfoundland. When the first province confederated some protection had to be given to the people of that province because the majority did not want divorce courts established there, and this place was found to be the most workable solution possible. Again, when Newfoundland entered confederation exactly the same thing ensued. I would be as happy as anybody else in this chamber to see divorce cases dealt with elsewhere. I do not like the job. It has been a miserable one and it is more miserable than ever because of what has happened lately, but at least I have tried to do what I can to make it as correct as possible and to make it easier for members here to rely in the committee on the sponsor of the bill when they come to vote on each particular measure. But as long as these provinces and the people in the provinces say no, and their wishes have to be taken first, then let us carry on with what is properly ours.
I support the recommendations in the committee's report. It has been a pleasure to be associated with you in that work and I hope the experiment of next year will turn out to be something we might write permanently into our rules.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under standing order 37 to explain what I consider to be a misrepresentation of something said earlier

by me today. The last speaker has referred to the fact that I made disparaging remarks about the legal counsel of the house. That is not true. What I said was that the legal counsel of the house has given advice when requested by the chairman or the committee on points of order. What I would wish for-it is certainly afforded to a court-is that the judge, or those in control of the committee, be continually supplied with this information instead of having to request it. I think there is a considerable difference there. We were certainly not casting any aspersions on Dr. Ollivier's record. He is certainly competent and although the advice he has given has not always been agreed with, he has certainly been competent and has been respected.

Then I rise on exactly the same point, under the section the hon. member brought up. The aspersions were not directed at Dr. Ollivier but at me for giving the committee legal advice. I am a lawyer and that is one of the reasons I suppose I was asked to chair that particular committee. I do give that advice when it will help hon. members. They are always free to challenge it, and I have never yet had a lawyer before me who has walked out of that committee unsatisfied with the conduct of the case.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is now speaking to the matter which is different from what was raised as an explanation.

Mr. Speaker, the presentation of this report affords me an opportunity of speaking on the procedure of the house, a matter which over the last three sessions, including this one, has given me a good deal of concern. I recognize at once that I am one of the new members of this house and when I came here I presumed that I as well as other hon. members would receive the same sort of instruction, and I was supplied with the standing orders of the house as well as the fourth edition of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms.
This evening we have heard from the last four successive speakers in this debate about divorce, private bills coming before the house, and the procedures applicable to private members. I think that subject has been pretty well exhausted and I do not intend to devote any time to that aspect of the business which comes before the house. I am more concerned, as I think most people are, with the conduct of the affairs of the public in this chamber, so I propose to deal with the procedures relating to government business.
I know that those of us who are here realize that this session began on January 14, approximately seven months ago. We are now nearing the end of the two summer months 79951-0-491J
Procedure Committee
of vacation, and I hope we are nearing the end of the business of this session. But may I say that the public little realize that this house is in session today. As far as I am concerned, some call my home and they are quite surprised when they do not find me there and learn that this house is still in session.
This report is the first step, and a very good step, toward shortening the sessions of the house. But it is a Very short step. I feel, as I believe almost everybody feels, that there is an unjustifiable waste of time in this house and a waste of the taxpayers' money in unnecessarily prolonging debate and, what I think is more serious still, an undue repetition of arguments on the various subjects which come before the house.
I well recall the first session of parliament, which began in May and the hope was expressed when it began that the work of that session would be completed before the summer was over. We found, as time went by, that this was not possible, and it was not until well into the month of September that that session prorogued. The cause of that was nothing more or less than a constant repetition of arguments time and time again during the debates of the house. I concede that we do not have a specific rule which deals with this matter. We do have a rule which deals with the repetition of argument and indulgence in irrelevancy by hon. members. However, I can find nothing in the rules which deals with one member repeating the arguments of another member, and I suggest to the committee, if and when it is set up in the next session, that consideration might well be given to some rule which would be effective in curbing what I consider to be an abuse of the privileges of the house.
In this connection I should like to put on the record an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail on August 18, 1958 and which is headed "Parliament's Garrulous Octet". I think it is significant and appropriate that I should refer to this editorial atthis time, because, although it relates to what occurred during the first session of this parliament, we have witnessed in this session of parliament tactics of filibuster by members of the C.C.F. party with respect to private bills of divorce. The editorial reads as follows:
There are 265 seats in the Canadian House of Commons. Only eight of them are occupied by members of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation. With eight votes C.C.F. can do little to make or change the decisions of the house on the issues which come before it. However, with eight voices and with the right to raise-

1 understand the rule is that it is not permitted to read editorials in

Procedure Committee
the house, especially when they cast reflections on the activities of some hon. members.

On the point of order, I consider that it is in order to read editorials. It has been done many, many times. The only possible objection could be that it might relate to a matter which is before the house.
I am pointing out that the rules do permit reading of an editorial as long as it is not intended to affect the decision of this house in a particular debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am unable to find the citation which deals with this matter. If my memory is correct, it is not in accordance with the practice to quote newspaper editorials dealing with the conduct of hon. members. It is in conformity with the practice to have the opinion of newspapers on matters discussed in the house, but it would not be permitted to read editorials in which the conduct of members or the conduct of the house is discussed.

If you consider this would be out of order, Mr. Speaker, because this is an editorial, then, inasmuch as I believe it is correct and that it does relate exactly what happened in the first session of this parliament, I am prepared to adopt these words as my own:
With eight votes C.C.F. can do little to make or change the decisions of the house on the issues which come before it. However with eight voices and with the right to raise them on every issue, it can do much to obstruct the house in reaching decisions. And this it seems to be doing deliberately at every opportunity.
The C.C.F. engage in silly and childish prolongation of debates. They get up, one after the other, and repeat one another's speeches. They do this to no apparent purpose, they say little that is constructive or useful, and they say little that is particularly critical. They just talk and talk until the other members want nothing more than to tell them to be quiet.
Last Friday, for instance, by the time the house adjourned for lunch at 1 p.m., four C.C.F. members had spoken among them, eight times and at least once on almost every subject which came up. After lunch, three of them made very long speeches, one made two very long speeches and took up almost the whole afternoon.
This has been going on for months. A look at the latest available index to Hansard shows that, between May 12 and June 30, C.C.F. leader Hazen Argue spoke on 81 different topics-more than did L. B. Pearson who spoke on 78, and less only than did the Prime Minister, who spoke on 99. Moreover, no C.C.F. member during that period spoke on fewer than 25 subjects and 3 spoke on more than 70. Compared, for example, with Conservative members, George Hees who spoke on 57 and D. S. Harkness who spoke on 21.
There is no possible reason for the C.C.F. bloc to talk so much, so often. It is abusing its parliamentary privilege. It is creating an atmosphere in which the government may well hesitate to bring forward new business because it will only give the C.C.F. another chance to prolong an

already over-worked session. Is there no way, short of another election, to shut these people up?
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) earlier in this debate talked about organization of the business of the house. I think that what is required is not so much organization of the business of the house but rather a little organization and discipline of the parties in the house so that these debates will not be dragged on endlessly and there will not be the repetition of which I complain.
What the C.C.F. group did in the first session I believe the Liberal party has continued to do in the second session and again in this third session of parliament. I believe this matter came to the fore when about two weeks ago the motion was moved to extend the hours of sitting of the house. That motion was strenuously opposed by both opposition parties. I think it would be better if hon. members opposite were, during the early part of the session, to think of the longer hours which will undoubtedly result from their making long and repetitive speeches.
This prolongation of debate has also been true of this session. In that connection may I refer to a Canadian Press dispatch of March 7 last referring to the progress that was made during the present session:
After seven weeks of commons sittings with relatively little to show for it, talk is beginning to be heard about parliament sitting all summer or perhaps going into a fall session. When parliament opened January 14, it was with the fairly confident expectation that it would be through by mid-June, give or take a week. But as the daily question periods consistently lengthened into an hour or more and as the unemployment debate dragged into 7| days, hope of hitting that target has faded. About the only concrete measure approved has been for emergency aid to prairie farmers with grain crops caught in the field by early fall snows. Most of the committee work is just getting under way. By far the major part of the government's legislative program remains to be considered. And the budget debate which will take another eight sitting days is still in the future. On top of that work is just beginning on the 1960-61 spending.
No one seems to have been able to determine accurately the cost to the country of keeping parliament in session but it obviously runs into thousands of dollars each day. Unnecessary prolongation of a session is therefore a waste of the taxpayers' dollars.
Another point I should like to make is that there appears nowhere in the rules any provision dealing with the questions which are directed to members of the government on the calling of the orders of the day. This practice seems to have grown up over the years but it is not a practice covered by oi dealt with by the rules. I suggest that if this is a good practice

and I believe it is-and it is to be entertained then it should be

covered explicitly under a rule. It should also be clearly provided that the questions which are asked of the ministry must be questions of immediate urgency. We have had many instances of the abuse of this privilege. In fact we had an instance today when a rather nonsensical question was asked of the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton).
I also believe that the question period should be limited in point of time. We have a precedent for that in that under standing order 39 (2) (b) there is a limitation placed upon the time to be devoted to starred questions on Wednesday. I think that period of time should be shortened although in my experience in the house it has never exceeded the hour allotted. Nevertheless I believe that period of one hour for starred questions might well be shortened.
I believe that questions which by practice or courtesy hon. members are allowed to direct to members of the government should also have a time limit imposed upon them and I see no reason why matters of immediate urgency cannot be dealt with and disposed of within a period of 15 minutes at the longest. On many occasions during this session the question period has exceeded an hour.
There is one other matter- on procedure to which I should like to make reference. I refer to the debate which has occasionally occurred on the various stages of an appropriation bill. As hon. members know, this bill relates to estimates presented in the house. Of course, I refer more particularly to the appropriation bill in connection with supplementary estimates. Under our procedure, supplementary estimates are subject to debate and on many occasions in the past the debate has been very extended. May I simply remind hon. members of the debate on supplementary estimates in March of this year, which was mentioned in the Canadian Press dispatch to which I made reference. As I recall it those supplementary estimates contained 20 items and some of them were quite small in amount. One of those items alone involved the expenditure of some $15 million, being the government's contribution to the municipalities in connection with the winter works incentive program. That item occasioned a debate of nine days, and the supplementary estimates in all consumed 14 days of debate. After that extensive and detailed examination of the estimates one would think that when the appropriation bill was presented to the house to give effect to the supplementary estimates which had already been considered and passed by the house there would be little or no debate on the bill. However, apparently in keeping with the designed policy of prolonging debate, we find
Procedure Committee
in this case the opposition again debated that bill through its various stages and a whole evening session of this house was taken up in the passage of that bill, a purely pro forme procedure of the house.
At this point it might be well to recall to mind the concern of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) at that time because of the attitude and the action of the opposition. May I quote from his remarks at that time as reported at page 1824 of Hansard:
Is it not about time that hon. members opposite gathered together some sense of responsibility with respect to the business of the house and the transaction of affairs that mean a great deal to the farmers of the country, to employed persons who will otherwise be threatened with unemployment and to many others in this country as well... As a result of their holding up this bill... 15 senior officials are sitting in my office right now who have come there for a budget meeting. I suppose my evening will be spent in the house listening to hon. members opposite fan the air with their incessant repetition.
I think the Minister of Finance pointed out at that time that in some 15 years of experience in this house he had never known of an appropriation bill being debated at all stages.
I have one other suggestion to make. When this committee is set up at the next session to continue its study of the procedure of the house I believe it would be well to enlarge its membership. At the present time I believe nearly all the members of that committee are members who have been in the house for a great many years. I think it would be well, and it would be helpful, if the membership of that committee were enlarged and there were added to its membership many of those members who have been here only a relatively short period of time. I think there is too much, shall I say, reliance placed upon precedents, habits and policies of the house and not enough consideration given to ways and means of dealing with the business expeditiously but carefully and with a reasonable amount of consideration. I think that those who have come to this house fresh from business, fresh from other positions where they have seen business done quickly, effectively and with due consideration would be of great help to this committee in devising ways and means whereby the rules could be amended and the business of the house transacted efficiently and expeditiously but also thoughtfully and carefully.

Mr. Speaker, may I rise just to express my surprise. Everybody has been talking on this motion and saying that there are too many long speeches, too much repetition, and all that I have heard today has been long speeches and repetition on a

Procedure Committee
motion that everybody wants to pass. Therefore, I think we should stop talking and move to something else.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just spoken could not have been here all day if he is of the opinion that the speeches have been repetitious. I have listened to the contributions of various hon. members on this particular matter throughout the day and I thought they placed before Your Honour many useful suggestions. After all, Mr. Speaker, when we are amending the rules of this house we are dealing with the rules of an institution which embodies almost a thousand years of the hopes and dreams of our people. This is not a thing that can be done lightly. This is not a project through which we should rush, but it is a project which requires careful consideration, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Spencer).
I was encouraged, as I am sure every other hon. member was encouraged, when the committee over which you, sir, presided presented these thoughtful proposals which were to be initiated on a trial basis and thus bring about adjustments which would be in keeping with the times. I was pleased to hear the suggestion of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), and his thought that progress would be made in dealing with this matter of divorce next year. I should like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure other hon. members will join me, in acknowledging our appreciation of the tremendous work he has done as chairman of the miscellaneous private bills committee.
There are two particular aspects of this situation with which I should like to deal very briefly. One arises out of the suggestions which are made from time to time to adjourn the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent importance under rule 26. This particular rule is a very useful rule, but I think it can be improved upon. The procedure followed at the present time is set out in subsection 2 of that rule, which says:
The member desiring to make such a motion rises in his place, asks leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance and states the matter.
Then he hands a written statement of the matter he proposes to discuss to the Speaker who decides whether or not it complies with the rule. Upon the ruling of the Speaker that the requisite conditions have been fulfilled, the debate begins at once. I suggest that that is not a good practice because it seems to me that if the matter is of such importance that the business of the house should be adjourned to discuss it there should be some sort of

notice or warning given so that hon. members who may wish to speak on that particular matter may gather their thoughts before they enter the debate.
In the British House of Commons provision is made for that very thing. I find by referring to the book "Honourable Members, A Study of the British Backbencher", by Peter G. Richards, a very distinguished member of the British parliament, that he says this:
Under standing order No. 9, the motion for the adjournment may also be used in an emergency to raise a matter of public importance-
I might explain that such a motion can be moved by either the opposition or the government. Then the debate does not take place immediately but at seven o'clock that night. In the intervening period hon. members who wish to take part in the debate can complete their preparations for doing so, which most certainly would add to the quality of the debate and would most certainly place before the public through the report of that debate the more considered views of members who had adequate time for preparation. I would commend to the committee consideration of this rule of the United Kingdom parliament when the committee studies these matters next year.
There is another point I should like to make in connection with private members' days. From time to time there arises in the course of the affairs of our nation matters which members feel should be discussed. They may be matters of extreme importance, but not of the complexity that would require prolonged debate. They are not matters of national interest that would require the adjournment of the business of the house under standing order 26. The British provide for this by means of what they call the daily adjournment of the debate. Under this provision there is a half-hour provided at the end of the day, three days a week, during which debates may take place on subjects drawn by lot from the numerous suggestions made by members of the house. These subjects are debated for half an hour. The usual procedure is that the mover or proposer of the subject speaks for 15 minutes, and then the minister under whose jurisdiction that particular matter falls or his parliamentary secretary replies. In that way many useful matters are ventilated and many useful discussions are initiated. I think perhaps if we gave thought to the provision of a similar rule in our house, it would permit, during the course of the session, many more matters to be discussed and it might save some time for discussion of other matters on private members' days. This half-hour is provided

in the United Kingdom on Mondays, Thursdays and Fridays, and I find this in Mr. Richards' book with reference to this subject:
This procedure may not be used to raise issues that would involve legislation, or for which the government has no responsibility.
Since this procedure has been adopted by the United Kingdom parliament it has come into great favour, as I understand it, and has proved to be a very useful device for enabling private members to place before the house and the country matters which they feel to be of great concern. Since time passes quickly I shall resume my seat after expressing the hope that during the deliberations of the committee next year the two suggestions I have made will be considered worthy of investigation.
