speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few minutes at my disposal, and I should like to make a few brief comments regarding the report of the special committee on the procedure of the house. That report contained four recommendations. The acceptance of two of those recommendations would have the effect of shortening by four days the sittings of the house. The other two recommendations mainly concerned matters of procedure and might-depending on how they were applied -speed up the dispatch of the business of the house.
Mr. Speaker, we are now at a critical stage in our parliamentary system. On the one hand, we are assailed by an ever growing quantity of increasingly complex public affairs.
In fact, we need only look into our copy of the estimates to see hundreds of items amounting to several billions of dollars, that the committee of supply is called upon to approve or reject.
How can a private member devote the required time to a serious consideration of those matters? I suggest that such consideration is far beyond the capacity of any ordinary brain and I think hon. members must recognize, in all humility, that they belong in that category. It therefore seems to me that we should accept the basic reforms suggested by several members today. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) suggested, among other things, that we should do away with details and that the debates of the house should be limited to the consideration of major issues. For my part, I would suggest- and this is my own personal opinion-that the special committee that will be set up
Procedure Committee
next year to study house procedure, look into the possibility of eliminating discussion in committee of legislation.
I would also suggest that detailed study of the estimates be done away with.
I suggest that the house study only the principle of the legislaion introduced by the government. Besides, it might be well if the debate in committee of supply were limited to consideration of the general policy of the department, i.e., the first item.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member allow a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Of course.
Does the hon. member think we should abolish closure?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: I did not understand the question.
Could the hon. member tell the house whether he thinks we should abolish closure?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member ought to let me make my speech as I see fit; if he wants to express his views, he will have an opportunity to do so.
As I was saying, there should be a limit to minute study of certain items. Suppose the committee of supply is asked to consider a vote of several million dollars for the building of a nuclear reactor. I wonder what point there is in submitting so technical a matter to a general assembly of laymen. It would certainly be better to refer such matters to a special committee of the house, a committee of supply, which could be divided into subcommittees on estimates, where experts would be called upon to give evidence. Such a committee could then submit its report either to a committee of the whole house, or to the house itself. I think that even if this report did not recommend the basic reforms that seem necessary, we should eventually come to recognize that principle by the very nature of things.
If we wish to preserve respect for our democratic parliamentary system, sooner or later we shall have to consider taking such decisions.
Before resuming my seat, I have only one more comment to make and it has to do with the remarks of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) who suggested that speeches delivered in this house should be restricted to 15 minutes. I do not share that

Procedure Committee
view, because, in my opinion, a speech cannot be reduced to simple mathematical proportions. Certain subjects can be discussed for hours without being fully covered, while others can be summarized in a few sentences. There are many historical examples to prove it and if I had more time at my disposal, I should like to quote a few of them.
Mr. Speaker, this may be an age of specialization and technique, but eloquence is still highly prized. And true eloquence, as Bossuet once said, must be based on simplicity and truth.
It was Tacitus who said:
Eloquence is like a flame: it requires matter to feed on, motion to excite it, and it brightens as it burns.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had a very useful discussion on matters of prime importance to the House of Commons, its method of conducting its business based on the rules. Quite a number of very useful suggestions have been advanced which I am sure will be used as a guide for the committee which will be set up next year.
The complexity of the problem appears as people discuss the matter, and some very thoughtful contributions were made during the course of the afternoon and evening by people who have been making a study of the rules and procedure of this house and of other legislative bodies. Careless generalizations often take the place of careful research and thought, and frequently all of us become a bit impatient with the parliamentary system and hope that matters can be speeded up. But on examination it is very difficult to say what matters should be dispensed with quickly and on what subjects time should be taken.
While the debate has been in progress I have been looking through a record that I have kept this year to see how the time has been utilized. I have a complete record, but I will not burden the house with it all. But it is interesting to note that in the first three months of this session the house used only 17 days of that time for legislative purposes. On those 17 days three special committees were set up; 10 items of legislation were started and nine were completed. Other days that were available for government purposes were consumed in discussion of supplementary estimates, interim supply and so forth. During the course of the three months the house did deal with the address

in reply to the speech from the throne, with most of the private members' days that are allotted by the rules, with I think four of the six supply motions, with interim supply, with supplementary estimates and with the budget debate.
When you look at those three months you see quite a considerable amount of the business of the house was done, but not business in the way of a great amount of legislation and no discussion of the main estimates in that period. But who is to say that there should not have been a debate on the speech from the throne or a lengthy debate on supplementary estimates or on interim supply, a practice which has grown up in recent years of using those two items for vehicles for rather lengthy debate? He would be very bold indeed to say that matters of importance to Canada were not discussed during those periods.
So I just draw to the attention of the house that short summary of what happened in the first three months of this session because it points up the complexity of the situation when you attempt by rules to determine the length of time which shall be spent on any one subject in the course of a parliamentary session. I suppose to a certain extent it depends on self-discipline, restricting the length of speeches which members may make, and on what was mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) earlier this afternoon, an allocation of time to various debates.
That can be done and has been done in this house session after session with regard to certain matters which have come before it. For example, we have had success in allotting time for debates on external affairs, either one days or two days. This year we allotted three and that was by arrangement, and then the debate came to a conclusion. By consultation and arrangement of allocation of time I think there is much which can be accomplished without a specific rule being laid down for debates which are before us. On the other hand if a controversial issue comes before the House of Commons no one can say how long a debate may last. It may go on for days or for weeks.
However, all of the discussion we have had today I think will be very useful and will serve as a guide to the committee which will be set up quite promptly next session, because we have now all admonished each other as to what should be done earlier on in the next session. If we have available to us in this modification of the rules, the opportunity of postponing the first private member's Thursday or the first private member's Monday and use days like that for the setting up of, say, special committees or bringing down legislation which is of urgency, then

we may advance some of these measures earlier in the session than has been done in the past. From my study of the sessions of the House of Commons over a long period of years I do not hold out much hope for shortening the sessions very much, but on the other hand we can increase the efficiency.

Yes. For tomorrow we will deal with supplementary estimates commencing with the one which was tabled today, No. 576 under agriculture, being the payment of an amount as a higher return for wheat used for human consumption in Canada to western grain producers, et cetera, followed by supplementary estimates in agriculture Nos. 500 to 504. As this department's estimates were completed some time ago it will be necessary to consider these supplemen-taries.
Then there is the supplementary estimate for external affairs, another department
Business of the House
which has been completed and was brought down today, No. 577 relating to a purchase of flour to be given to the United Nations relief and works agency. If we complete those there is the supplementary estimate No. 498 under finance dealing with the salaries of civil servants.
Then we have a problem which we may have to face tomorrow, but which we do not have to decide tonight, namely whether or not interim supply should be considered tomorrow. I am in the hands of the people on the other side of the house as to that. If the house will complete all the estimates and pass the usual appropriation act with not too long a debate, as was mentioned by my hon. friend behind me, within the next two or three days, it will not be necessary to have interim supply tomorrow night. On the other hand, if the business of the house takes more time than the next two or three days, then in order that people in the employ of the government and others may be paid we might have to have interim supply tomorrow. But I leave it to the good sense of the house as to what we do and we can make that decision tomorrow.
